topic: Zero-shot generalization in reinforcement learning
text:
IDEA: Training reinforcement learning agents using a dynamically adaptive curriculum of tasks with rigorously defined, progressively increasing complexity yields significantly improved zero-shot generalization on unseen, out-of-distribution tasks compared to training on a fixed, static dataset of diverse tasks.

BACKGROUND: Current reinforcement learning (RL) methods struggle to generalize zero-shot to novel tasks outside their training distribution, limiting real-world applicability. Although prior approaches leverage diverse static datasets or data augmentation for generalization, they often overlook the potential of systematically structured curricula that adaptively guide learning through task complexities grounded in theoretically sound difficulty metrics. Addressing this gap could foster more robust policy representations that transfer effectively to unseen environments.

APPROACH: We propose a curriculum learning framework where tasks are ordered and dynamically selected based on validated, theoretically justified complexity measures—such as task entropy, environment transition uncertainty, and agent learning progress—rather than naive proxies like baseline success rates. A task scheduler monitors performance and advances the curriculum only upon stable mastery, ensuring adaptive progression. This is implemented in Meta-World v2 and Procgen benchmarks, with the curriculum controlling environment parameters (e.g., obstacle density, horizon length) to modulate complexity, while a static group trains on a randomly shuffled fixed set spanning the same complexity range, both sharing identical RL algorithms (e.g., SAC or PPO) and training budgets.

EXPERIMENT: We evaluate zero-shot generalization on carefully defined held-out Meta-World and Procgen tasks explicitly designed to be out-of-distribution by systematically varying complexity and task structure beyond the training range. Success metrics include average normalized return and task success rate aggregated over multiple seeds, with rigorous statistical testing to detect at least a 10% performance improvement by the curriculum group over the static baseline, while controlling for total environment interactions and sample complexity.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior work focusing on static diversity or data augmentation, our approach introduces a theoretically grounded, dynamically adaptive curriculum that explicitly links task complexity to learning progression, thereby promoting the development of transferable abstract representations and inductive biases that underpin improved zero-shot generalization in RL policies.

topic: Zero-shot generalization in reinforcement learning
text:
IDEA: Incorporating explicit causal structure priors via modular graph neural network policies improves zero-shot generalization of reinforcement learning agents to unseen environment dynamics by enabling structured reasoning over causal factors.

BACKGROUND: Zero-shot generalization in reinforcement learning remains a critical challenge, as policies trained under fixed dynamics often fail to transfer effectively to environments with altered or novel physical parameters. Existing approaches leveraging representation learning or relational inductive biases have shown limited and inconsistent gains, lacking explicit causal reasoning that could promote robustness to distribution shifts in environment dynamics.

APPROACH: We propose a modular policy architecture based on graph neural networks (GNNs) where nodes correspond to semantically meaningful causal factors—such as limbs, joints, and contacts—and edges encode domain-informed causal relations. The policy is trained with proximal policy optimization (PPO) on source environments with fixed dynamics, and zero-shot evaluated on variants with systematically perturbed physical parameters (mass, friction, joint stiffness). An ablation replacing the GNN with a capacity-matched multilayer perceptron (MLP) isolates the effect of causal structure priors.

EXPERIMENT: We evaluate zero-shot generalization on the DeepMind Control Suite’s Walker and Cheetah tasks under controlled perturbations, and on the Meta-World ML45 robotic manipulation benchmark with diverse unseen object dynamics. Performance is quantified by average episodic return over 50 zero-shot episodes, comparing causal-GNN and MLP baselines matched for capacity and relational biases. Statistical significance is assessed via paired t-tests (p < 0.05), with a required minimum 15% improvement over the strongest non-causal baseline and consistent ablation drops to confirm causal prior efficacy.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior work focusing on implicit relational biases or abstract representation learning, this study explicitly encodes hypothesized causal structures within policy architectures and rigorously quantifies their impact on zero-shot transfer under systematically controlled dynamics shifts. It also provides a theoretical framing on the identifiability and validity of causal priors in RL generalization, advancing beyond heuristic modularization toward scientifically grounded causal reasoning in policy design.

topic: Zero-shot generalization in reinforcement learning
text:
IDEA:  
Incorporating unsupervised causal structure discovery into reinforcement learning agents enhances zero-shot generalization across procedurally generated environments more effectively than contrastive representation learning alone.

BACKGROUND:  
Current reinforcement learning (RL) agents struggle to generalize zero-shot to unseen environments due to reliance on correlational rather than causal features in high-dimensional observations. While contrastive representation learning improves robustness by learning invariant features, it does not explicitly capture underlying causal mechanisms governing environment dynamics, limiting transfer under distribution shifts common in procedurally generated domains.

APPROACH:  
We propose augmenting RL agents with an unsupervised causal discovery module that jointly learns latent state embeddings and infers causal graphs representing environment dynamics using methods inspired by DAG-GNN and variational causal factor disentanglement. This causal embedding is integrated into the policy network, replacing or augmenting standard encoders. To ensure rigorous evaluation, we include capacity-matched baselines with contrastive learning (e.g., CURL), random/shuffled causal graphs, and data augmentation-only agents, controlling for confounding factors.

EXPERIMENT:  
We will train agents on a subset of ProcGen Benchmark games (e.g., 10/16) and Crafter environments, then evaluate zero-shot performance on held-out ProcGen games and unseen Crafter seeds using average episode return, minimum return, and performance variance. Statistical significance will be assessed over 5+ random seeds with multiple comparison corrections, aiming for ≥10% improvement over contrastive baselines in ≥75% of held-out environments to confirm the hypothesis; failure to surpass by >5% falsifies it.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior work focused on contrastive or augmentation-based representations, this study explicitly integrates unsupervised causal discovery into RL in high-dimensional, procedural settings and rigorously ablates causal inductive biases. It addresses challenges of causal factor identifiability and nonstationarity in RL training, providing the first comprehensive evaluation of causal structure learning’s impact on zero-shot generalization in challenging, large-scale procedurally generated domains.

topic: Zero-shot generalization in reinforcement learning
text:
IDEA:  
Training offline reinforcement learning agents with a curriculum of dynamically evolving reward functions, implemented via principled reward relabeling consistent with the static dataset, leads to significantly improved zero-shot generalization to unseen environment variants compared to agents trained with static or fixed-mixed reward functions.

BACKGROUND:  
Offline RL agents often overfit to static reward signals in fixed datasets, limiting their ability to generalize zero-shot to unseen environment variants such as novel maze layouts or object configurations. Existing techniques focusing on representation learning or similarity-based methods improve generalization to some extent but do not leverage reward function dynamics. Introducing controlled variability in reward signals during training could encourage policies to be robust to reward perturbations, potentially enhancing zero-shot generalization in offline RL.

APPROACH:  
We propose a reward evolution schedule that systematically applies parametric reward perturbations—such as stochastic combinations of sparse and dense rewards, varying subgoal emphasis, and auxiliary pseudo-rewards derived from environment state features—via a principled offline reward relabeling framework ensuring consistency with the original dataset distribution. This evolving reward schedule is integrated into Conservative Q-Learning updates, enabling the agent to optimize a distribution over related reward functions without requiring new data collection. Critical ablations include static mixtures of multiple reward functions and fixed auxiliary rewards to isolate the dynamic schedule’s effect.

EXPERIMENT:  
We evaluate on the D4RL AntMaze (e.g., antmaze-medium-diverse-v0) and Meta-World ML1 (e.g., ML1-Button-Press-v2) offline benchmarks by measuring zero-shot success rates and normalized cumulative rewards on carefully curated unseen environment variants (novel maze layouts and object positions) without fine-tuning. Statistical significance is assessed over multiple seeds, with the hypothesis supported if the evolving reward agent achieves at least 15% absolute improvement over the best baseline (static reward CQL, similarity-function augmented RL, and data augmentation-based representation learning) and falsified if it fails to outperform by 5%.

NOVELTY:  
This work is the first to systematically introduce and evaluate dynamically evolving reward functions within strictly offline RL via consistent reward relabeling, disentangling reward dynamics from representation changes or static reward diversity. Unlike prior work focusing on representation or similarity learning, our approach directly manipulates reward signals in offline data to promote policy robustness and generalization, validated rigorously with new ablations and theoretical motivation linking reward perturbations to environment variation.

topic: Zero-shot generalization in reinforcement learning
text:
IDEA:  
Training reinforcement learning agents on a curriculum of progressively more abstract simulated environments, combined with intermediate domain adaptation steps, improves zero-shot generalization to real-world robotic tasks more than training on diverse, fully detailed simulated environments without curriculum progression.

BACKGROUND:  
Zero-shot generalization remains a critical challenge in reinforcement learning (RL), particularly for sim-to-real transfer where policies trained in simulation often fail to generalize due to visual and physical discrepancies. Existing methods like domain randomization and diversity-based training improve robustness but can lead to overfitting to irrelevant visual details or inefficient learning. Abstraction-based curricula, which progressively increase environment complexity from low-dimensional states to richer visuals, promise to foster more transferable, task-relevant representations but lack systematic empirical validation against strong baselines that isolate curriculum and abstraction effects.

APPROACH:  
We propose an RL training framework where agents learn via a curriculum starting from simplified, low-dimensional state abstractions of Procgen environments and incrementally incorporate pixel-level details and physical realism, guided by a scheduler controlling complexity parameters such as texture granularity, object count, and distractors. Representation learning is regularized with a bottleneck layer to enforce abstraction. We integrate intermediate validation on proxy tasks and use domain adaptation techniques (e.g., feature-level alignment) before evaluating zero-shot on high-fidelity real-world robot manipulation tasks from the Real Robot Challenge (RRC) dataset. Baselines include agents trained on fully detailed Procgen environments without curriculum, curriculum without abstraction, domain randomization approaches, and low-dimensional state-only training.

EXPERIMENT:  
Train Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) agents under four conditions—(1) Curriculum-Abstract, (2) Detailed-Diverse, (3) Curriculum-Detailed, and (4) Domain Randomization—using Procgen environments for simulation. Evaluate zero-shot transfer via average episodic return over 100 episodes and generalization gap between simulation validation and RRC real-world tasks. Success requires Curriculum-Abstract agents to outperform Detailed-Diverse by at least 15% with p < 0.05 (bootstrap CI); falsification occurs if Detailed-Diverse or other baselines exceed Curriculum-Abstract by this margin or show no significant difference.

NOVELTY:  
This work explicitly integrates progressive abstraction-based curricula with domain adaptation and intermediate validation to systematically isolate the effect of environment abstraction and curriculum scheduling on zero-shot sim-to-real transfer. Unlike prior work that focuses on domain randomization or static abstractions, it proposes a theoretically grounded, mechanistic curriculum that gradually bridges the sim-to-real gap, supported by rigorous baselines and controls across modalities and training paradigms.

topic: Foundation models for genomics and single-cell biology
text:
IDEA:  
Pretraining foundation models jointly on multi-omics single-cell data integrating chromatin accessibility and gene expression will significantly improve prediction of cell-type-specific regulatory element activity compared to genome-only pretrained models.

BACKGROUND:  
Accurate prediction of cell-type-specific enhancer activity is critical for understanding gene regulation in complex tissues, yet existing models pretrained solely on genome sequence or chromatin accessibility often fail to capture coordinated regulatory signals that emerge from multiple molecular layers. Single-cell multi-omics datasets that profile chromatin accessibility alongside matched gene expression provide a unique opportunity to learn richer, context-aware representations of regulatory elements, addressing limitations of genome-only approaches.

APPROACH:  
We propose to develop a multimodal Transformer foundation model that integrates DNA sequence context with chromatin accessibility and single-cell RNA expression embeddings from paired multi-omics datasets (e.g., SHARE-seq). This model will be pretrained with a masked token prediction objective across modalities to capture cross-modal regulatory dependencies. A genome-only baseline Transformer will be trained on sequence and chromatin accessibility data without expression information, enabling a controlled comparison.

EXPERIMENT:  
Both models will be fine-tuned and evaluated on independent cell-type-specific enhancer activity data from single-cell MPRA assays (Cao et al., 2022), with performance measured by area under the precision-recall curve (AUPR) and area under the ROC curve (AUROC). Statistical significance of improvement will be assessed by paired bootstrap tests, requiring at least a 5% absolute increase in mean metrics for the multi-omics model to confirm the hypothesis, while failure to improve by 2% will falsify it.

NOVELTY:  
This work rigorously isolates the benefit of multi-omics integration during pretraining through matched datasets, controlled architectures, and intermediate modality ablations, and introduces a novel cross-modal masked token objective within a Transformer architecture to explicitly model coordinated regulatory signals from single-cell multi-omics data—advancing beyond prior genome-only or unimodal models for regulatory element prediction.

topic: Foundation models for genomics and single-cell biology
text:
IDEA:  
Pre-training foundation models on matched multimodal single-cell data (RNA, ATAC, and protein) enables superior prediction of cell-type-specific gene regulatory networks compared to single-modality models, as validated by held-out CRISPR perturbation experiments.

BACKGROUND:  
Accurately inferring gene regulatory networks (GRNs) at single-cell resolution remains a critical challenge due to the complexity of gene regulation and limitations of single-modality data. Existing methods often rely on either transcriptomic or epigenomic inputs, which capture only partial regulatory signals and may miss cross-modality interactions essential for robust GRN reconstruction. Multimodal single-cell technologies now provide paired measurements that, if integrated effectively, could reveal comprehensive regulatory mechanisms but have not been rigorously evaluated in a foundation model framework with causal perturbation validation.

APPROACH:  
We propose a cross-modal transformer-based foundation model that jointly encodes RNA-seq, ATAC-seq, and CITE-seq protein data from the same cells using modality-specific token embeddings and shared attention layers. The model will be pre-trained via a masked token prediction objective extended with cross-modality attention mechanisms to capture regulatory dependencies, followed by supervised fine-tuning to predict GRN edges defined from perturbation effect sizes. Ablation studies and overfitting controls will disentangle modality contributions and ensure biological robustness.

EXPERIMENT:  
We will pre-train on the 10x Multiome PBMC dataset (GEO GSE158055) combined with matched CITE-seq protein data from the Seurat PBMC dataset, and validate on held-out Perturb-seq CRISPR knockout data from Adamson et al. (GEO GSE90063). Performance will be benchmarked against single-modality foundation models (RNA-only, ATAC-only, protein-only), classical single-modality GRN inference methods (e.g., SCENIC, GRNBoost), and multimodal feed-forward baselines, using area under the precision-recall curve (AUPR) and area under the ROC curve (AUROC) for perturbation-induced target gene prediction. Statistical significance will be established via bootstrapped confidence intervals over multiple perturbation targets.

NOVELTY:  
This work uniquely integrates multimodal single-cell data into a foundation model with a novel cross-modal transformer architecture and rigorous masked token pre-training designed to capture causal regulatory signals across modalities. Unlike prior GRN inference approaches or unimodal foundation models, it is explicitly validated against high-quality perturbation datasets, with detailed modality ablations and noise controls, providing clear evidence of the added value of multimodal integration for gene regulatory network reconstruction.

topic: Foundation models for genomics and single-cell biology
text:
IDEA:  
Foundation models pretrained on carefully aligned and denoised multimodal single-cell data (transcriptomics, epigenomics, and proteomics) will predict cell-type-specific gene regulatory networks (GRNs) with significantly higher accuracy and biological fidelity than unimodal models trained on transcriptomics alone, as demonstrated by held-out perturbation benchmarks.

BACKGROUND:  
Accurate inference of cell-type-specific GRNs from single-cell data remains a critical challenge, particularly due to the complex, multimodal nature of gene regulation involving transcriptional, epigenetic, and proteomic layers. Existing methods typically leverage unimodal transcriptomic data, limiting their ability to capture the full regulatory landscape. Integrating multimodal single-cell measurements in foundation models promises richer representations but requires robust alignment and rigorous evaluation against causal perturbation data to validate improvements.

APPROACH:  
We will develop a transformer-based multimodal foundation model pretrained on harmonized embeddings derived from matched single-cell transcriptomics, chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq), and surface proteomics (CITE-seq) datasets—specifically 10x Genomics Multiome PBMC and brain cortex samples plus Human Cell Atlas CITE-seq data. To address missing modalities, batch effects, and noise, we will apply advanced cross-modal alignment using joint manifold learning (e.g., mutual nearest neighbors), modality-specific normalization, and imputation strategies rather than naive concatenation. The model will be trained with masked token prediction and cross-modal contrastive objectives to capture regulatory dependencies. Baseline comparisons will include unimodal transformer models trained solely on gene expression, and established GRN inference methods like SCENIC and GRNBoost2, matched for cell types and preprocessing.

EXPERIMENT:  
We will evaluate predictive performance on held-out perturbation datasets including Perturb-seq (Dixit et al., 2016) and CRISPRi screens (Replogle et al., 2022) that profile transcription factor and enhancer perturbations in matched cell types. Metrics will include AUPR and AUROC for identification of perturbed gene targets, plus network sparsity, biological pathway enrichment, and robustness under modality ablation. Statistical significance will be assessed via bootstrapping, and negative controls with randomized edges will be included to control for overfitting and spurious correlations.

NOVELTY:  
This work explicitly integrates multimodal single-cell data through principled alignment and transformer-based representation learning tailored for gene regulatory inference, moving beyond prior unimodal or naive multimodal concatenation approaches. By coupling rigorous multimodal pretraining with causal perturbation benchmarks and comprehensive evaluations—including ablations and network plausibility—this study provides the first systematic demonstration that foundation models with multimodal inputs yield meaningful gains for cell-type-specific GRN prediction.

topic: Foundation models for genomics and single-cell biology
text:
IDEA:  
Foundation models pretrained on integrated multi-omic single-cell datasets can predict novel cell-type-specific regulatory elements with higher accuracy and biological interpretability than models trained solely on bulk genomic data or single-modality single-cell data.

BACKGROUND:  
Accurately identifying cell-type-specific regulatory elements such as enhancers is critical for understanding gene regulation and cellular function, yet bulk genomic data obscure cell-type heterogeneity. While recent models leverage either bulk epigenomic profiles or single-modality single-cell data, they often fail to capture the complex interplay among chromatin accessibility, gene expression, and DNA methylation at cellular resolution, limiting prediction accuracy and mechanistic insight.

APPROACH:  
We propose pretraining transformer-based foundation models on large-scale multi-omic single-cell datasets from the Human Cell Atlas, integrating scATAC-seq, scRNA-seq, and single-cell methylation via modality-specific encoders and a shared latent space using masked token prediction and contrastive learning. Comparative models pretrained on bulk ENCODE data and single-modality single-cell data will be trained and fine-tuned on experimentally validated cell-type-specific enhancer prediction tasks with a classification head, incorporating rigorous controls to isolate the contribution of multi-omic single-cell integration.

EXPERIMENT:  
Models will be evaluated on held-out cell types and genomic loci using enhancer labels from single-cell resolution atlases such as SCREEN and single-cell STARR-seq in hematopoietic cells, measuring AUPRC and AUROC for enhancer prediction; ablation studies will include single-modality single-cell and bulk multi-omic pretrained models to test the hypothesis that multi-omic single-cell pretraining yields ≥5% absolute AUPRC improvement, with motif recovery and concordance to known transcription factor binding sites assessed for interpretability.

NOVELTY:  
This work is the first to systematically integrate multi-omic single-cell modalities within a foundation model framework to enhance prediction of cell-type-specific regulatory elements, providing a theoretically grounded approach to disentangle biological signal from technical noise and modality discordance, and establishing clear empirical evidence that multi-omic single-cell integration surpasses bulk and single-modality models in both accuracy and biological relevance.

topic: Foundation models for genomics and single-cell biology
text:
IDEA:  
Foundation models pre-trained on integrated multi-omics single-cell data (scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq) provide superior predictive accuracy for cell-type-specific regulatory element activity compared to single-modality models, as validated by quantitative CRISPR perturbation assays.

BACKGROUND:  
Predicting cell-type-specific regulatory elements is critical for understanding gene regulation and disease mechanisms but remains challenging due to complex, context-dependent interactions. While single-modality models leverage either transcriptomic or chromatin accessibility data, their predictive power is limited by modality-specific biases and incomplete regulatory context. Multi-omics integration via foundation models offers a promising avenue to capture complementary biological signals across modalities, yet rigorous validation against functional perturbation data is lacking.

APPROACH:  
We propose to develop a transformer-based foundation model that jointly encodes paired scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq single-cell profiles from the Human Cell Atlas using cross-modal attention mechanisms, enabling integrated cell representations. The model will be fine-tuned to predict regulatory element activity linked to specific cell types, incorporating comprehensive preprocessing including batch correction, modality-specific normalization, and strategies to impute missing modalities. Prediction performance will be quantitatively assessed against CRISPR perturbation effect sizes derived from Perturb-seq and SHARE-seq datasets, incorporating negative controls and batch-aware evaluation.

EXPERIMENT:  
We will train the multi-omics foundation model on the Human Cell Atlas multi-modal data and compare it against (1) single-modality foundation models trained on either scRNA-seq or scATAC-seq alone, and (2) classical machine learning baselines such as Random Forests and convolutional neural networks trained on matched single-modality data. Predictive accuracy will be evaluated using Pearson correlation coefficients between predicted regulatory activity and experimentally observed log fold-changes in gene expression from CRISPR perturbations, with r ≥ 0.7 indicating strong performance. Additional metrics such as Spearman correlation and calibration of uncertainty estimates will supplement evaluation. Validation will explicitly control for batch effects, modality coverage, and include negative perturbation controls.

NOVELTY:  
This work rigorously integrates multi-omics single-cell data using a foundational transformer architecture with explicit cross-modal attention and theoretically motivated preprocessing, differentiating it from prior single- or dual-modal transformers like scBERT and CellFormer. Crucially, it couples integrated representation learning with well-controlled CRISPR perturbation benchmarks, establishing a concrete falsification criterion and biologically interpretable validation framework that advances predictive modeling of regulatory elements beyond existing approaches.

topic: Federated learning with heterogeneous and non-IID data
text:
IDEA: Incorporate a client-side meta-learning framework that adaptively re-weights local updates based on gradient statistics and parameter discrepancies to more effectively mitigate client-drift in federated learning with extreme non-IID data than variance-reduction methods like SCAFFOLD.

BACKGROUND: Federated learning suffers from client-drift when local data distributions are heterogeneous and non-IID, leading to slow convergence and degraded global model accuracy. Existing approaches such as SCAFFOLD use control variates to reduce variance, but often do not explicitly adapt local update contributions based on client-specific data heterogeneity or dynamic local training behavior. Addressing this gap can enable more robust aggregation under extreme data skew.

APPROACH: We propose a bilevel optimization framework where each client maintains a meta-learner that observes its local gradient statistics and the divergence between its local and the global model parameters to update adaptive weighting coefficients on local gradients. The inner loop performs weighted local SGD, while the outer loop uses gradient-based meta-learning (e.g., MAML or Reptile variants adapted to federated settings) to update these weights, emphasizing updates aligned with the global objective and thus reducing client-drift.

EXPERIMENT: We evaluate on CIFAR-10 and Fashion-MNIST partitioned into extreme non-IID splits where each client holds data primarily from 2 out of 10 classes with imbalanced distribution. Baselines include FedAvg, FedProx, and SCAFFOLD. Metrics are global test accuracy after 200 rounds and convergence speed measured by rounds to reach 80% of final accuracy. Additionally, we quantify client-drift via local-global model divergence and update variance. Success requires our method to outperform SCAFFOLD and FedProx by ≥5% accuracy and converge ≥20% faster under matched computation and communication budgets.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior variance-reduction methods that statically correct local updates, our approach dynamically learns adaptive weights via client-side meta-learning informed by local training dynamics and model divergence, with theoretical analysis providing convergence guarantees and client-drift bounds. This principled meta-learning adaptation under resource constraints and extreme heterogeneity distinguishes our work from existing adaptive weighting or control variate approaches.

topic: Federated learning with heterogeneous and non-IID data
text:
IDEA: Incorporate dynamically adapted personalized model architectures via constrained neural architecture search on each client to reduce client-drift and improve convergence speed in federated learning with heterogeneous, non-IID data.

BACKGROUND: Federated learning on heterogeneous and non-IID data suffers from client-drift, causing slow and unstable convergence when global models are trained with fixed shared architectures. Existing solutions like FedAvg, SCAFFOLD, and knowledge distillation improve training stability but do not leverage structural model personalization, which could better capture local data peculiarities while maintaining global generalization.

APPROACH: We propose Dynamic Personalized Architecture Federated Learning (DPA-FL), where clients start from a lightweight base CNN and adapt their architectures during local training using a neural architecture search constrained by local validation loss and a complexity budget. The server aggregates only shared base layers while personalized architecture components remain local, enabling structural adaptation to client-specific data heterogeneity. We also include controlled baselines such as federated NAS without personalization and static personalized architectures to isolate the benefits of dynamic adaptation.

EXPERIMENT: We evaluate on heterogeneous, non-IID CIFAR-10 with Dirichlet partitioning (α=0.1) and FEMNIST datasets, measuring (1) final global accuracy on a held-out aggregate test set, (2) average client test accuracy for personalization benefit, and (3) convergence speed defined by communication rounds and wall-clock time to reach 90% of final accuracy. Statistical significance tests (e.g., paired t-tests or Wilcoxon signed-rank) and detailed profiling of computational and communication overhead on realistic client hardware are performed to validate gains and feasibility.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior personalized FL methods that use fixed architectures or knowledge distillation without structural changes, DPA-FL uniquely integrates dynamic NAS constrained by complexity and validation signals to enable per-client architectural adaptation while preserving shared parameters for global knowledge, supported by theoretical analysis linking architecture adaptation to client-drift mitigation and convergence stability.

topic: Federated learning with heterogeneous and non-IID data
text:
IDEA:  
Personalizing federated learning aggregation weights by incorporating clients’ data heterogeneity metrics—computed via privacy-preserving, scalable proxies of statistical distribution divergence—yields improved global model accuracy and convergence compared to uniform, performance-based, or randomized weighting schemes on heterogeneous and non-IID datasets.

BACKGROUND:  
Federated learning suffers from degraded global model performance and slow convergence when clients’ data are heterogeneous and non-IID, as traditional aggregation schemes treat all client updates uniformly or rely solely on performance-based heuristics that overlook distributional differences. Existing approaches either ignore quantifying heterogeneity explicitly or require costly, privacy-sensitive computations of data distributions, limiting their practical applicability and theoretical understanding of personalized weighting benefits.

APPROACH:  
We propose a heterogeneity-aware aggregation method where each client locally estimates a privacy-preserving, computationally lightweight heterogeneity score by measuring the statistical distance—using approximate Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) with random Fourier features or Earth Mover’s Distance (EMD) on feature embeddings—from a server-provided global distribution summary (e.g., a compressed histogram or representative sample embedding). These scalar heterogeneity metrics are securely communicated to the server, which computes normalized inverse heterogeneity-based weights combined with client data sizes, controlled by a tunable exponent, to personalize aggregation in FedAvg. This design maintains standard federated protocols, respects client privacy, and is robust to sample size variability and resource constraints.

EXPERIMENT:  
We evaluate on CIFAR-10-LT and FEMNIST datasets partitioned over 100 clients with realistic heterogeneous non-IID splits, comparing against baselines: (1) FedAvg uniform weighting, (2) performance-based weighting proportional to local validation accuracy, and (3) statistically matched non-personalized randomized weighting that mimics the heterogeneity-weight distribution. Metrics include final global test accuracy after 200 rounds, convergence speed to 90% peak accuracy, and stability quantified by variance in accuracy over multiple (≥5) independent runs with statistical significance testing (e.g., paired t-tests).

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior work that either ignores explicit heterogeneity quantification or requires expensive, privacy-risky computations, we develop a practical, scalable, and privacy-preserving method to estimate heterogeneity metrics on resource-constrained clients, integrating these into personalized aggregation weights. Our theoretical framing clarifies how inverse heterogeneity weighting balances contribution quality and diversity, and our rigorous falsification criterion using controlled randomized baselines sets a new standard for evaluating personalization benefits in federated learning under data heterogeneity.

topic: Federated learning with heterogeneous and non-IID data
text:
IDEA: Incorporating personalized data augmentation strategies, optimized per client via automated search, reduces client-drift and improves global model performance more effectively than global knowledge distillation in heterogeneous federated learning with non-IID data.

BACKGROUND: Federated learning on heterogeneous and non-IID client data suffers from client-drift, where local models diverge due to disparate data distributions, slowing convergence and degrading global model accuracy. Existing mitigation strategies like global knowledge distillation provide uniform teacher signals but do not adapt to individual client data characteristics or address the root cause of local distribution shifts. There is a need for personalized approaches that adapt augmentation to local data to robustly reduce drift and enhance learning.

APPROACH: We propose a Personalized Data Augmentation (PDA) framework that dynamically profiles each client's local data distribution and employs automated augmentation policy search (via reinforcement learning or Bayesian optimization) to tailor augmentations such as geometric transforms, cropping, and noise injection to maximize local data diversity and model generalization. PDA integrates this search lightweightly and periodically on client devices, contrasting with a Local-Global Knowledge Distillation (LGKD) baseline where clients receive distilled global teacher signals, and a FedAvg baseline without drift mitigation. We additionally include two critical ablations: a global (non-personalized) augmentation baseline and PDA without automated search to isolate the impact of personalization and policy optimization.

EXPERIMENT: We evaluate on two widely used heterogeneous federated datasets—LEAF’s FEMNIST partitioned by writer (image domain) and Google Speech Commands V2 partitioned by speaker (audio domain)—measuring (i) global model test accuracy after fixed communication rounds, (ii) client-drift quantified by the average cosine distance between local and global model update vectors per round, and (iii) convergence speed as rounds to reach 90% of final accuracy. The hypothesis is supported if PDA significantly outperforms LGKD and FedAvg by >2% accuracy, reduces client-drift by at least 10%, and converges faster consistently across datasets.

NOVELTY: This work uniquely combines personalized, automated data augmentation policy search with federated learning to directly reduce client-drift, a departure from prior work relying primarily on uniform global knowledge distillation or control variate methods. By incorporating strong baselines and ablations and providing theoretical insight into how personalized augmentation shapes local update distributions, it advances practical, scalable drift mitigation tailored to client heterogeneity in both image and speech domains.

topic: Federated learning with heterogeneous and non-IID data
text:
IDEA: Incorporating personalized meta-learning modules with adaptive inner-loop updates into each client model reduces client-drift and accelerates global model convergence on highly heterogeneous, non-IID federated data more effectively than control variate methods like SCAFFOLD.

BACKGROUND: Federated learning on heterogeneous and non-IID data suffers from client-drift, where local model updates diverge due to skewed data distributions, slowing global convergence and degrading accuracy. Existing control variate approaches like SCAFFOLD mitigate drift via correction terms but do not explicitly personalize local training dynamics, limiting adaptability under diverse client conditions.

APPROACH: We propose a personalized federated learning framework that embeds a lightweight Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML)-style inner loop within each client’s local training, enabling rapid adaptation to local data distribution shifts while jointly updating global parameters. Unlike FedAvg or SCAFFOLD, this meta-learning module explicitly models client-specific adaptation, minimizing update divergence without requiring control variates. We also include personalized FL baselines without meta-learning and a non-federated meta-learning baseline to isolate the contribution of meta-personalization in a federated context.

EXPERIMENT: We evaluate on FEMNIST (partitioned by writer with skewed label distributions) and Google Speech Commands (split by speaker), measuring (a) final global test accuracy after 200 communication rounds, (b) communication rounds to reach target accuracies (75% for FEMNIST, 85% for Speech Commands), and (c) client-drift diagnostics such as gradient variance and update divergence. Performance gains of ≥3% accuracy and ≥20% faster convergence compared to SCAFFOLD across 5+ seeds will support our hypothesis; no significant improvement falsifies it. Computational overhead and scalability on resource-constrained clients will also be profiled.

NOVELTY: This work uniquely integrates personalized meta-learning inner loops within federated optimization to directly learn client adaptation dynamics that reduce drift, providing a theoretically motivated alternative to control variate correction. Unlike prior meta-learning FL approaches, we formalize conditions under which meta-personalization improves convergence speed in highly heterogeneous settings and empirically validate its benefits against both classical and personalized baselines with detailed client-drift analysis.

topic: Protein structure prediction beyond AlphaFold
text:
IDEA: Incorporate experimentally derived cross-linking mass spectrometry (XL-MS) distance restraints as explicit constraints into a retrained AlphaFold-Multimer model architecture tailored for flexible and transient protein-protein interfaces, to improve interface prediction accuracy for transient complexes with high-quality XL-MS data.

BACKGROUND: Despite AlphaFold-Multimer’s advances in protein complex prediction, accurately modeling flexible and transient protein-protein interfaces remains challenging due to conformational heterogeneity and limited training on experimental restraint data. XL-MS provides sparse, experimentally validated inter-residue distance constraints that can inform flexible interfaces but are underutilized in end-to-end deep learning models. Integrating XL-MS constraints directly into model retraining could overcome limitations of purely inference-time or physics-based docking approaches, enhancing predictive accuracy for transient complexes.

APPROACH: We propose architectural modifications to AlphaFold-Multimer’s input and loss functions to incorporate XL-MS cross-linked residue pairs as explicit distance priors with uncertainty-aware upper bounds (~30 Å), using a multi-task loss combining structure prediction and cross-link satisfaction penalties. Retraining will apply transfer learning techniques with XL-MS-annotated transient complexes from combined XL-MS datasets (e.g., PRIDE Archive PXD014704) and Docking Benchmark 5.5 transient subset, employing data augmentation and regularization to prevent overfitting given limited XL-MS data. Controls include vanilla AlphaFold-Multimer and HADDOCK docking with XL-MS restraints.

EXPERIMENT: We will evaluate interface accuracy improvements using Interface RMSD (iRMSD) and DockQ scores against known complex structures, plus quantify XL-MS restraint satisfaction rates, comparing retrained and baseline models on a curated test set of transient complexes with high-confidence XL-MS and solved structures. Statistically significant improvements (≥1.0 Å iRMSD reduction, ≥0.1 DockQ increase, and ≥20% fewer violated cross-links; p < 0.05, paired t-test) will confirm the hypothesis; failure to improve or degradation will falsify it.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior inference-only or physics-based integration of XL-MS data, this work explicitly retrains a state-of-the-art deep learning model to internalize sparse, noisy XL-MS constraints, addressing uncertainty and flexibility at the architectural and loss function levels. This approach leverages transfer learning to overcome data scarcity and exploits model inductive biases to robustly incorporate experimental restraints during structure prediction, advancing beyond current post-hoc or fine-tuning methods.

topic: Protein structure prediction beyond AlphaFold
text:
IDEA: Integrate a variational autoencoder-based latent space module into AlphaFold-like architectures to explicitly model protein dynamic ensembles, thereby improving prediction accuracy and ensemble diversity of intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) beyond static structure predictions.

BACKGROUND: While AlphaFold 2 and related methods excel at predicting static protein structures, intrinsically disordered regions remain challenging due to their inherent conformational heterogeneity and lack of stable tertiary structure. Current approaches either output a single static model or generate ensembles without leveraging deep learning representations, limiting accuracy and biological interpretability of IDR predictions.

APPROACH: We extend AlphaFold’s architecture by incorporating a VAE latent space module that samples multiple plausible conformers per residue from AlphaFold’s internal representations, producing explicit structural ensembles for IDRs. The model is trained using a multi-task loss combining RMSD to experimental NMR ensemble conformers and agreement with DisProt disorder annotations, encouraging both structural fidelity and accurate disorder region classification.

EXPERIMENT: Using a curated dataset of proteins from DisProt v9.1 paired with corresponding NMR ensemble data from the Protein Data Bank, we will benchmark our method against (1) AlphaFold 2’s standard static predictions, (2) ensemble methods like ENSEMBLE and Flexible-Meccano, and (3) AlphaFold-generated ensembles via stochastic dropout sampling as a control. Success metrics include ensemble-average RMSD to NMR conformers for IDRs (target <3.5 Å), AUC for disorder region classification (>0.85), and ensemble diversity measured by average pairwise RMSD within predicted ensembles. Statistical significance will be evaluated (p<0.01) to confirm improvements.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior ensemble or disorder prediction methods that lack integrated deep learning of conformational heterogeneity or rely on external sampling, our approach leverages AlphaFold’s rich internal representations within a generative VAE framework to explicitly model structural dynamics. This synergistic training on both structural ensembles and disorder annotations enables improved fidelity and interpretability of IDR predictions beyond currently available static or ensemble-only methods.

topic: Protein structure prediction beyond AlphaFold
text:
IDEA: Integrating experimentally-informed NMR ensemble restraints with enhanced sampling molecular dynamics applied to AlphaFold2-predicted structures will improve the identification and characterization of catalytically relevant transient conformational states, as validated by quantitative agreement with NMR relaxation dispersion and biochemical kinetics.

BACKGROUND: While AlphaFold2 produces highly accurate static protein structures, it does not capture functionally important transient conformations that underlie enzyme catalysis. Current integrative approaches often rely on conventional MD or static models, lacking rigorous incorporation of dynamic experimental data such as NMR relaxation dispersion, which directly report on millisecond-timescale conformational exchange. There is a critical need for methods that combine AlphaFold accuracy with physics-based sampling and experimental restraints to generate realistic dynamic ensembles reflecting catalytically relevant states under physiological conditions.

APPROACH: Starting from AlphaFold2 predicted models of enzymes with well-characterized dynamic catalysis (e.g., Cyclophilin A 2CPL and DHFR 1RX2), we will perform enhanced sampling MD (Gaussian accelerated MD and well-tempered metadynamics) integrated with time-averaged ensemble restraints derived from NMR chemical shifts and relaxation dispersion data using maximum entropy approaches. This iterative protocol ensures the conformational ensemble converges to NMR-consistent populations without overfitting. The resulting ensembles will be analyzed for transient active-site loop motions and correlated to experimentally measured catalytic rates.

EXPERIMENT: We will benchmark against three baselines—raw AlphaFold2 static structures, conventional equilibrium MD without enhanced sampling or restraints, and enhanced sampling MD without experimental restraints—using datasets with extensive NMR data (BMRB IDs linked to 2CPL and 1RX2) and kinetic assays. Success metrics include ≥20% reduction in RMSD between simulated and experimental chemical shifts and relaxation rates, transient state populations within ±5% of NMR-derived values, and Pearson’s correlation r > 0.8 between simulated conformational kinetics and biochemical turnover rates, assessed across multiple replicates with rigorous statistical validation. Failure to exceed these improvements over baselines falsifies the hypothesis.

NOVELTY: This work explicitly addresses limitations of static AlphaFold models by leveraging experimentally derived dynamic restraints to guide enhanced sampling, going beyond prior post-processing or coarse ensemble refinement methods. The integration of sophisticated NMR relaxation data into advanced MD sampling frameworks with iterative convergence and statistical rigor establishes a novel, reproducible pipeline for dynamic functional structure prediction not previously demonstrated at this level of quantitative validation.

topic: Protein structure prediction beyond AlphaFold
text:
IDEA: Incorporate high-confidence crosslinking mass spectrometry (XL-MS) distance restraints as soft constraints into AlphaFold 3’s multimer pipeline to improve biologically relevant interface prediction for multi-protein complexes with weak evolutionary signals.

BACKGROUND: Although AlphaFold 3 achieves remarkable accuracy in protein complex structure prediction, its reliance on evolutionary co-variation limits performance on complexes with sparse multiple sequence alignments and weak inter-protein evolutionary signals. Experimental XL-MS data can provide complementary spatial restraints but has not been systematically integrated into AlphaFold 3’s deep learning folding framework to enhance interface modeling in such challenging cases.

APPROACH: We propose modifying AlphaFold 3’s multimer model by encoding experimentally derived high-confidence XL-MS crosslinks as soft upper-bound distance restraints during the network’s structure optimization phase, fine-tuning the model on a curated dataset of complexes with matched structural and XL-MS data. This integration is designed to leverage the complementary, though noisy and sparse, experimental information without overriding AlphaFold’s learned priors, thereby improving interface accuracy for complexes lacking strong co-evolutionary signals.

EXPERIMENT: Using the Docking Benchmark 5.5 subset with weak evolutionary coupling complexes and corresponding high-confidence XL-MS data from the PRIDE repository (e.g., Schweppe et al., 2019), we will model each complex with (AF3+XL-MS) and without (AF3 alone) restraints, comparing interface prediction performance via DockQ scores, Interface RMSD, and interface residue precision/recall; random and ablated restraint controls will validate the specificity of XL-MS contributions. A statistically significant ≥10% average DockQ improvement in the weak-signal subset will confirm the hypothesis, while non-significant or negative results will falsify it.

NOVELTY: This work uniquely integrates sparse, noisy XL-MS distance restraints directly into AlphaFold 3’s end-to-end deep learning pipeline through novel soft restraint encoding and targeted fine-tuning, contrasting with prior methods that apply experimental data post hoc or use separate docking frameworks, thus advancing hybrid modeling by synergistically combining experimental spatial data with deep learning-based structure prediction in a principled manner.

topic: Protein structure prediction beyond AlphaFold
text:
IDEA: Integrating dynamic conformational ensembles generated via enhanced sampling from AlphaFold 3 static models improves the accuracy of predicting functionally relevant allosteric states, as validated by stronger correlations to experimental activity shifts compared to static or MD-only models.

BACKGROUND: While AlphaFold 3 excels at predicting static protein structures, it does not capture the dynamic conformational heterogeneity essential for allosteric regulation, limiting functional inference from static models alone. Existing methods either rely on single static snapshots or purely physics-based simulations without leveraging deep learning-derived structural priors, leaving a gap in accurately predicting allosteric states linked to function.

APPROACH: We will develop a computational pipeline that integrates AlphaFold 3 predictions with enhanced sampling methods such as Markov State Models and variational autoencoders to generate dynamic conformational ensembles reflecting allosteric transitions. These ensembles will be analyzed using physics-informed free energy calculations and machine learning regression models trained on allosteric datasets to predict functional activity shifts and binding affinities.

EXPERIMENT: Using experimentally validated allosteric enzyme datasets from the Allosteric Database (ASD) and NMR-derived ensembles from the Protein Ensemble Database (PED), we will compare predictions from (a) AlphaFold 3 static models, (b) AlphaFold-Multimer for complexed proteins, (c) standalone MD simulations, and (d) our ensemble-integrated approach. Success will be measured by significant improvements in Pearson correlation (r > 0.7, p < 0.01) and ROC-AUC (>0.85) for classifying active versus inactive allosteric states against experimental data, with rigorous statistical validation via cross-validation and bootstrapping.

NOVELTY: This work uniquely combines state-of-the-art AlphaFold 3 structural predictions with advanced enhanced sampling and machine learning to explicitly model dynamic allosteric conformational landscapes, moving beyond static or MD-only approaches. By grounding ensemble generation with orthogonal experimental validations and establishing a formal falsifiable hypothesis linked to functional outcomes, it advances the theoretical and practical integration of deep learning and dynamics for functional protein structure prediction.

topic: Topological methods for high-dimensional data analysis
text:
IDEA:  
Integrating persistent spectral graph features with neural network embeddings through a principled multi-view learning framework improves clustering accuracy on high-dimensional single-cell RNA-seq data beyond either method alone.

BACKGROUND:  
Accurately clustering high-dimensional single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) data remains challenging due to complex nonlinear gene expression patterns and intrinsic biological heterogeneity. Existing methods leveraging neural network embeddings (e.g., variational autoencoders) capture nonlinear structure but may miss complementary multiscale topological and geometric features encoded by persistent spectral graph methods. A principled fusion of these complementary representations could enhance biological cluster recovery, yet this integration and its scalability remain underexplored.

APPROACH:  
We first extract persistent spectral graph features by applying the persistent combinatorial Laplacian to simplicial complex filtrations constructed from scRNA-seq gene expression data, capturing multiscale topological and geometric information. Separately, we train a neural network embedding (e.g., scVI variational autoencoder) to learn nonlinear latent representations. Instead of simple concatenation, we integrate these feature sets using a multi-view learning approach—such as canonical correlation analysis (CCA), deep multi-view representation learning, or joint graph-embedding optimization—to fuse complementary information while mitigating feature incompatibility. Dimensionality reduction and subsampling strategies ensure scalability and reproducibility.

EXPERIMENT:  
We benchmark clustering performance on the 10x Genomics PBMC 68k dataset and the Tabula Muris Senis scRNA-seq dataset, using normalized mutual information (NMI) and adjusted Rand index (ARI) against ground-truth cell type labels. We conduct repeated stratified data splits preserving biological heterogeneity and apply paired statistical tests (t-tests with p < 0.05) over bootstrap replicates to assess whether the integrated model significantly outperforms the best individual baseline (persistent spectral graph or neural embeddings alone), as well as PCA-based and non-topological concatenation controls. Ablation studies isolate the contribution of each component.

NOVELTY:  
This work advances beyond prior scRNA-seq topological or neural embedding analyses by providing a theoretically justified, scalable, and rigorously validated multi-view integration of persistent spectral graph features with neural embeddings. It demonstrates, for the first time, that such principled fusion yields statistically significant improvements in clustering accuracy on large, biologically complex single-cell datasets.

topic: Topological methods for high-dimensional data analysis
text:
IDEA:  
Incorporate scalable higher-order persistent homology features (H1 and H2) as principled, normalized augmentations to gene expression data prior to UMAP embedding, to improve cluster separation of high-dimensional biological single-cell RNA-seq datasets beyond standard UMAP and competitive baselines.

BACKGROUND:  
Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data are high-dimensional and heterogeneous, challenging traditional dimensionality reduction and clustering methods to faithfully capture underlying cellular subpopulations. While UMAP excels at manifold learning, it often overlooks global topological features like loops and voids that reflect biological heterogeneity, and existing topological analyses rarely integrate higher-order homology with manifold embeddings in a scalable, interpretable manner.

APPROACH:  
We propose computing higher-order persistent homology (H1 and H2) on subsampled or landmark-based Vietoris-Rips filtrations of scRNA-seq gene expression point clouds to extract persistence landscapes or persistence images as vectorized topological summaries. These features will be normalized and fused with gene expression data via a kernel-based weighting scheme before UMAP embedding, ensuring balanced joint representation. Rigorous controls including randomized-topology feature concatenations will isolate topological contributions from dimensionality effects.

EXPERIMENT:  
We will evaluate cluster separation on two benchmark datasets with known cell-type labels: the 10x Genomics PBMC 10k and Zeisel et al.’s Mouse Brain cortex datasets. Methods compared are baseline UMAP, Topo-UMAP (our method), and PHATE. Success will be quantified primarily by statistically significant (p < 0.05, paired t-test) and meaningful (>5% absolute) improvements in silhouette scores on 2D embeddings over multiple seeds, complemented by ARI, NMI, embedding stability analyses, and negative controls.

NOVELTY:  
This work advances prior TDA-scRNA-seq studies by addressing computational scalability of higher-order persistent homology on large datasets, developing a theoretically justified and kernel-based integration framework for heterogeneous features, and implementing rigorous controls to disentangle topological signal from embedding artifacts, providing the first principled demonstration of improved cluster separability via combined topological-manifold learning embeddings in this domain.

topic: Topological methods for high-dimensional data analysis
text:
IDEA: Integrating persistent spectral graph features derived from multiscale topological filtrations with learned deep neural network embeddings yields a statistically significant improvement in classification accuracy on heterogeneous high-dimensional biomedical datasets compared to either feature set alone.

BACKGROUND: High-dimensional biomedical data, such as single-cell transcriptomics and multi-omics cancer profiles, exhibit complex geometric and topological structures that challenge standard machine learning methods. While deep neural networks provide powerful learned embeddings, they often fail to explicitly capture multiscale topological information, and existing topological data analysis methods rarely integrate with deep representations robustly or scalably. Bridging these complementary perspectives can improve classification robustness and interpretability in noisy, heterogeneous biomedical contexts.

APPROACH: We propose to extract persistent spectral graph features by constructing scalable Vietoris–Rips filtrations on dimensionality-reduced data representations and computing persistent combinatorial Laplacian eigenvalue summaries capturing multiscale topological and geometric information. These fixed-length spectral summaries will be concatenated with embeddings learned from state-of-the-art deep neural networks (feedforward or graph-based depending on data modality), followed by joint training of downstream classification layers with regularization and normalization to prevent overfitting. We will rigorously assess the stability and complementarity of these features through ablation studies and randomized controls.

EXPERIMENT: Performance will be evaluated on two heterogeneous biomedical datasets: the Human Cell Atlas PBMC single-cell RNA-seq dataset for cell type classification, and the TCGA Pan-Cancer multi-omics dataset for cancer subtype classification. Classification accuracy on held-out test sets—averaged over multiple train-test splits—will be the primary metric. Success is defined as a statistically significant (p < 0.01, paired t-test) accuracy improvement of at least 3% by the integrated model over both individual baselines. Failure to surpass the best baseline by at least 1% consistently will falsify the hypothesis.

NOVELTY: This work advances beyond prior applications of topological data analysis and persistent spectral methods by developing scalable and robust computational pipelines for persistent spectral features on large biomedical datasets, theoretically grounding their complementarity with deep embeddings, and rigorously validating their integrated use with carefully controlled experiments. Unlike prior studies that apply topological features or deep embeddings in isolation, we demonstrate their synergistic benefit for high-dimensional biomedical classification tasks with reproducible and statistically rigorous evaluation.

topic: Topological methods for high-dimensional data analysis
text:
IDEA:  
Incorporating explicitly constructed higher-order simplicial complexes up to dimension four in topological data analysis significantly enhances the detection of functional clusters in high-dimensional single-cell RNA-seq data compared to classical Mapper and nonlinear dimensionality reduction clustering methods.

BACKGROUND:  
Current topological data analysis (TDA) methods for high-dimensional biological data, such as Mapper, primarily rely on 1- and 2-simplices (edges and triangles) and thus capture only pairwise or triplet relationships, potentially missing critical multi-way interactions underlying complex cellular heterogeneity. However, biological systems often exhibit higher-order combinatorial interactions, motivating the need for scalable methods that incorporate 3- and 4-simplices to better resolve functional clusters and continuous trajectories in noisy, high-dimensional single-cell transcriptomic data.

APPROACH:  
We propose Higher-Order Simplicial Complex Analysis (HOSCA), which extends classical Mapper by constructing simplicial complexes that explicitly include tetrahedra (3-simplices) and 4-simplices from multivariate intersections of cover sets derived from diffusion map embeddings. Persistent cohomology computations on these enriched complexes will extract stable higher-dimensional topological features that capture multi-way biological interactions. Clusters are then identified through a reproducible pipeline mapping persistent features to discrete clusters, validated via bootstrap testing and internal controls restricting to 2-simplices and synthetic benchmarks.

EXPERIMENT:  
We will evaluate HOSCA on the 10x Genomics PBMC 68k dataset and the Mouse Brain Atlas (Zeisel et al., 2015), both containing annotated cell types and continuous trajectories, comparing cluster outputs to classical Mapper (KeplerMapper/giotto-tda with optimized parameters) and UMAP/t-SNE plus Louvain clustering baselines. Performance will be quantitatively assessed using adjusted Rand index (ARI) and normalized mutual information (NMI) against gold-standard labels, with statistically significant improvements defined as p < 0.01 (paired bootstrap) and at least 10% better ARI/NMI over Mapper and 5% over UMAP/t-SNE.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior work that limits higher-order interactions to visualization or pairwise simplices, HOSCA systematically constructs and analyzes higher-dimensional simplices up to dimension four, with explicit computational strategies addressing scalability and robustness in large-scale biological data. This approach uniquely integrates advanced persistent cohomology on enriched simplicial complexes to capture biologically meaningful multi-way relationships, providing a theoretically justified and empirically validated framework for improved functional cluster detection beyond existing Mapper-based TDA and nonlinear embedding methods.

topic: Topological methods for high-dimensional data analysis
text:
IDEA:  
Integrate a topology-preserving regularizer based on bottleneck distance minimization into contrastive self-supervised learning to produce latent embeddings whose persistent homology shape descriptors exhibit improved robustness and classification of topological features compared to raw input and standard embedding baselines.

BACKGROUND:  
High-dimensional data often contain meaningful topological structures (e.g., loops, branches) that standard embedding or dimensionality reduction methods may distort or fail to preserve, limiting the utility of topological data analysis (TDA) like persistent homology. Existing approaches either apply persistent homology directly on raw data or on arbitrary embeddings without explicitly enforcing topological preservation, leading to unstable or less interpretable shape descriptors. Developing scalable, topology-aware representation learning methods that maintain or enhance these intrinsic features remains an open challenge.

APPROACH:  
We propose training contrastive self-supervised encoders (e.g., ResNet-50 for image-like data, specialized autoencoders for scRNA-seq) augmented with a batch-wise topological regularizer that minimizes the bottleneck distance between persistence diagrams of mini-batches in input and latent spaces. Efficient approximations—such as landmark-based Vietoris-Rips filtrations and vectorized persistence summaries computed at controlled frequencies—will ensure computational feasibility. This encourages latent embeddings to retain critical topological features during representation learning, enabling more robust persistent homology analyses on the learned manifolds.

EXPERIMENT:  
We will evaluate on three publicly available datasets with validated topological structures: MNIST (784D pixel space, known loops), DeepMind 3D Shapes (synthetic latent factors with ground-truth topology), and Human Cell Atlas single-cell RNA-seq (branching trajectories). Baselines include: (a) persistence diagrams directly from raw data, (b) latent spaces from standard contrastive learning (SimCLR), and (c) embeddings from UMAP and t-SNE with default parameters. Robustness is measured by bottleneck distance stability across multiple noise and subsampling perturbations (with repeated trials at varying levels) and classification accuracy of topological labels (e.g., loop or cluster membership) using k-NN on persistence landscapes. Controls on embedding dimension and reconstruction error will disentangle topology preservation from representational capacity. Success requires ≥10% improved diagram stability and non-inferior classification accuracy; failure occurs if improvements fall within 5% or classification accuracy drops >10% relative to input space.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior work that applies TDA post hoc or uses topological constraints in deterministic autoencoders without contrastive objectives, our method uniquely combines contrastive self-supervised learning with scalable topological regularization explicitly minimizing bottleneck distances in mini-batches, supported by rigorous computational strategies and theoretical justification for global topology preservation from local constraints. This framework enables a principled trade-off between topology preservation and representation quality, advancing robust high-dimensional shape analysis beyond existing manifold learning and TDA integration methods.

topic: Deep learning emulators for climate model acceleration
text:
IDEA: Deep learning emulators trained on harmonized multi-model CMIP6 ensembles with domain adaptation generalize significantly better to out-of-distribution extreme climate regimes from CORDEX regional simulations than emulators trained on single-model outputs.

BACKGROUND: Accurately emulating subgrid-scale processes and extreme event dynamics is critical for accelerating climate model simulations and improving climate risk assessments. Existing deep learning emulators often rely on single-model data, limiting their ability to generalize across diverse climate regimes and extreme events, which exhibit substantial inter-model variability and domain shifts. Addressing this gap requires rigorous multi-model training and validation frameworks explicitly designed to handle domain shifts and evaluate robustness on unseen extreme climates.

APPROACH: We develop convolutional LSTM-based deep learning emulators trained on carefully preprocessed, bias-corrected, and regridded multi-model CMIP6 data encompassing key variables relevant to extremes (surface temperature, precipitation, soil moisture). To enhance cross-model robustness, we incorporate adversarial domain adaptation techniques that encourage invariant feature representations. Emulators map coarse-scale predictors to fine-scale climate diagnostics and are trained with stratified multi-model sampling protocols to preserve inter-model variability.

EXPERIMENT: We perform cross-model validation by training emulators on CMIP6 outputs from five global climate models (CESM2, MPI-ESM1.2, HadGEM3, GFDL-CM4, IPSL-CM6A-LR) and testing on independent high-resolution CORDEX simulations of North American and European heatwaves and heavy precipitation extremes. Evaluation metrics include root mean squared error (RMSE) and continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) with accompanying uncertainty quantification and statistical significance testing. The hypothesis is falsified if the multi-model domain-adapted emulator does not achieve at least a 10% improvement in RMSE and CRPS over the best single-model emulator on these out-of-distribution extremes under strict data leakage controls.

NOVELTY: This work uniquely combines rigorous data harmonization, multi-model ensemble training, and adversarial domain adaptation to explicitly tackle domain shifts between global CMIP6 and regional CORDEX extreme event data. Unlike prior studies that focus on within-model emulation or single-model training, we rigorously quantify generalization to unseen extreme regimes across models, providing statistically robust evidence and theoretical grounding for multi-model training benefits in climate model acceleration.

topic: Deep learning emulators for climate model acceleration
text:
IDEA:  
Deep learning emulators trained on multi-model CMIP6 climate simulation ensembles will generalize more accurately across distinct climate regimes in predicting subgrid-scale turbulence parameterizations than emulators trained on single-model datasets, demonstrating statistically significant improvements in normalized root mean squared error (NRMSE) on out-of-distribution tests.

BACKGROUND:  
Accurately representing subgrid-scale (SGS) processes remains a critical challenge in climate modeling, as classical parameterizations like the dynamic Smagorinsky model suffer from limited flexibility and generalization across diverse regimes. Prior deep learning efforts have focused largely on single-model emulators trained on individual datasets, limiting robustness and transferability when applied to novel climates or different Earth system models. Addressing inter-model distribution shifts and enhancing emulator generalization is essential for accelerating climate simulations without sacrificing fidelity.

APPROACH:  
We propose training convolutional neural network (CNN) emulators with residual and batch normalization layers on combined, standardized SGS outputs (e.g., viscosity and diffusivity fields) pooled from multiple CMIP6 models (CESM2, MPI-ESM1.2, UKESM1-0-LL), incorporating explicit domain adaptation techniques such as climate-regime-specific feature normalization and model identity embeddings to mitigate inter-model biases. Single-model CNN emulators and classical baselines—including the dynamic Smagorinsky model and a multi-model linear regression—will serve as comparisons, with a rigorous evaluation stratified by spatially and temporally separated climate regimes to ensure out-of-distribution generalization assessment.

EXPERIMENT:  
Models will be trained on spatial-temporal patches from historical simulations and tested on held-out future scenario data and spatially blocked climate regimes (tropics, mid-latitudes, polar) from the CMIP6 ensemble, with normalized root mean squared error (NRMSE) on SGS viscosity and diffusivity as the primary metric. Statistically significant improvements (p < 0.05 via spatially aware permutation tests) of at least 10% NRMSE reduction for the multi-model emulator over the best single-model emulator across all regimes will confirm the hypothesis; failure to meet this threshold or consistent regime-specific degradation will falsify it.

NOVELTY:  
This study advances beyond previous single-model deep learning emulation by explicitly integrating multi-model training with principled domain adaptation to overcome inter-model distributional shifts, employing spatial-blocked evaluation and spatially dependent significance testing to robustly validate out-of-distribution performance gains. This combination of multi-model ensemble learning and rigorous, spatially aware validation represents a novel methodological contribution to climate model acceleration and SGS parameterization emulation.

topic: Deep learning emulators for climate model acceleration
text:
IDEA: Physics-informed neural network (PINN) emulators that explicitly enforce conservation laws produce more stable and physically consistent long-term climate simulations than purely data-driven deep neural network (DNN) emulators.

BACKGROUND: Climate model acceleration via deep learning emulators of subgrid-scale processes is promising but challenged by instabilities and unphysical drift during multi-decadal simulations. Existing data-driven approaches often lack physical constraints, resulting in degraded long-term stability and fidelity, limiting usability for climate projection and scenario analysis.

APPROACH: We develop and integrate a PINN emulator that embeds hard constraints on conservation of energy, mass, and momentum—such as divergence-free velocity fields and thermodynamic balance equations—directly into the network architecture and loss functions. This PINN and a baseline DNN emulator will be coupled within the Community Earth System Model (CESM) framework to replace traditional parameterizations, enabling controlled long-term simulations driven by both emulators.

EXPERIMENT: Using the CESM Large Ensemble (CESM-LE) dataset for training and validation with temporally and spatially stratified splits, we will compare baseline DNN and PINN emulators on subgrid-scale flux prediction RMSE and multi-decadal climate simulation stability metrics—including normalized mean squared error (NMSE) of global mean surface temperature and zonal wind profiles, boundedness of energy variables, and absence of drift—evaluated over 30-year coupled runs and statistically tested via paired t-tests across ensemble members; generalizability will be further assessed with ERA5 reanalysis data.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior work focused on purely data-driven emulators or limited physics constraints, this study rigorously incorporates multiple fundamental conservation laws as hard constraints within a PINN framework and demonstrates end-to-end integration into a full Earth system model for stable multi-decadal climate simulations, providing a theoretically justified and empirically validated pathway to improve emulator robustness and physical fidelity.

topic: Deep learning emulators for climate model acceleration
text:
IDEA:  
Develop deep learning emulators for subgrid-scale oceanic and atmospheric turbulence that enforce hard physical conservation laws via architecture and constrained optimization, achieving more accurate and physically consistent predictions of SGS viscosity and diffusivity than unconstrained neural networks.

BACKGROUND:  
Accurate representation of subgrid-scale (SGS) processes in climate models remains a critical challenge that limits predictive skill and physical fidelity, particularly for turbulent shear flows and cloud convection. While deep neural networks have shown promise in emulating SGS parameterizations, existing approaches rely primarily on data fitting with soft penalty terms and lack rigorous enforcement of conservation laws, leading to physically inconsistent or unstable predictions. Incorporating true hard constraints on kinetic energy and scalar variance budgets could improve both accuracy and closure in climate emulators.

APPROACH:  
We propose a neural network emulator architecture augmented with explicit hard constraint mechanisms, such as constrained optimization via Lagrange multipliers or projection layers that enforce conservation laws exactly at each training iteration. Inputs include local velocity fields, strain rates, and density gradients, with outputs predicting SGS viscosity and diffusivity fields. The loss function integrates mean squared error with constraint satisfaction guarantees, and ablation studies will compare hard constraints, soft penalty terms, and unconstrained models under identical data splits.

EXPERIMENT:  
The hypothesis will be tested using high-resolution LES datasets from the Johns Hopkins Turbulence Database (JHTDB) for stratified turbulent shear flows and finely resolved Cloud System Resolving Model (CSRM) outputs for convective SGS processes. Model accuracy will be quantified by normalized root mean squared error (NRMSE) of SGS viscosity and diffusivity predictions against LES ground truth on held-out test sets, while physical consistency will be evaluated by assessing kinetic energy and scalar variance budget closure errors in time-integrated simulations driven by emulator outputs. Success requires ≥10% NRMSE improvement over unconstrained DNN baselines and conservation budget errors within 5% of LES benchmarks.

NOVELTY:  
This work advances beyond prior physics-informed SGS emulation by implementing genuine hard constraint enforcement methods rather than relying on loss penalties, providing rigorous theoretical guarantees of conservation law satisfaction.
