The comprehensive experimental framework includes new intermediate baselines and integrates emulator outputs with dynamical core simulations to directly assess physical closure, offering novel insights into the trade-offs and practical benefits of hard-constrained deep learning emulators for climate model acceleration.

topic: Deep learning emulators for climate model acceleration
text:
IDEA:  
Deep learning emulators leveraging a multi-scale physically consistent framework can accurately reproduce emergent cloud-radiation feedbacks from high-resolution LES climate data within 5% error of global energy budgets, while surpassing traditional parameterizations in both accuracy and computational efficiency across diverse climate regimes.

BACKGROUND:  
Accurate, efficient representation of subgrid cloud-radiation interactions remains a critical bottleneck in climate modeling, limiting fidelity and scalability of Earth system projections. Traditional parameterizations in models like CAM6 often trade physical realism for computational tractability and struggle to generalize across regimes. Recent advances suggest deep learning emulators trained on LES data can accelerate modeling, but rigorous validation, theoretical grounding, and reproducible benchmarking remain insufficient to establish their reliability and generalizability.

APPROACH:  
We propose a convolutional neural network combined with temporal convolutional networks (CNN-TCN) trained on LES outputs from the DOE E3SM project, aggregated to CAM6 grid scales via a physically consistent upscaling methodology that preserves energy budget closure. The model inputs atmospheric states and radiative flux profiles to emulate cloud-radiation feedbacks dynamically. We enforce physical constraints in training loss functions and rigorously test generalization on independent datasets sampled across latitudes, seasons, and climate states.

EXPERIMENT:  
Using CAM6 standard parameterizations and the Brenowitz & Bretherton (2018) DL emulator as baselines, we evaluate on held-out LES-driven test sets spanning multiple climate regimes. Metrics include relative error (<5%) and RMSE reduction (>20%) on annual mean TOA and surface shortwave and longwave radiation budgets, alongside runtime benchmarks (including preprocessing and communication) measured on standardized HPC GPU nodes, requiring at least a 2× speedup over CAM6 per timestep. Failure to meet accuracy or efficiency thresholds or to generalize without retraining falsifies the hypothesis.

NOVELTY:  
This work integrates a rigorous multi-scale upscaling framework and physically constrained CNN-TCN architecture to address non-stationarity and scale-interactions explicitly, producing a reproducible benchmarking protocol grounded in climate theory. It meaningfully advances beyond prior DL emulators by demonstrating robust generalization and simultaneous improvements in physical fidelity and computational efficiency verified across diverse climate regimes.

topic: Emergent communication in multi-agent systems
text:
IDEA: Multi-agent systems equipped with heterogeneous sensory modalities develop more efficient and robust emergent communication protocols than homogeneous systems, due to improved complementary information fusion under constrained bandwidth and noisy conditions.

BACKGROUND: Coordinating multi-agent systems (MAS) in complex, noisy environments requires efficient communication protocols that can leverage diverse sensory inputs. While prior work explores emergent communication and homogeneous sensor setups, it remains an open problem whether sensory heterogeneity intrinsically enhances communication efficiency and robustness beyond simply increasing total sensory information. This research addresses how asynchronous multi-modal fusion affects emergent protocols under realistic noise and bandwidth constraints.

APPROACH: We propose a multi-agent communication framework integrating a Transformer-based attention encoder per agent that asynchronously fuses temporally aligned visual and spatialized audio inputs from the MPE-Visual-Audio dataset extension. Agents with heterogeneous sensor allocations (non-overlapping vision or audio) are compared against homogeneous groups receiving either singular modalities or the full sensory union, controlling for total sensory input volume. Communication messages are bandwidth-limited and learned via a modified Deep Communicative Q-Network (DCQN) with an Emergent Language Protocol (ELP) to enable task-driven selective encoding.

EXPERIMENT: Agents will be trained on a cooperative navigation task in the Multi-Agent Particle Environment with calibrated Gaussian noise injected into sensory inputs and communication channels following a standardized protocol. Success metrics include normalized communication bandwidth usage (bits per episode per task complexity), task success rate (goal achievement within fixed time), and robustness measured by the slope of success rate degradation across increasing noise variances. Statistical testing with effect size (Cohen’s d > 0.8) will validate whether heterogeneous MAS outperform homogeneous baselines by at least 15% in success rate and use 20% less bandwidth.

NOVELTY: This work uniquely combines asynchronous multi-modal sensory fusion with an attention-based Transformer encoder within a constrained bandwidth emergent communication framework, rigorously controls for sensory information volume to isolate heterogeneity effects, and standardizes noise injection and efficiency metrics—advancing beyond prior MAS communication studies that focus solely on homogeneous modalities or unconstrained channels.

topic: Emergent communication in multi-agent systems
text:
IDEA:  
In multi-agent reinforcement learning, dynamically evolving communication protocols augmented with agents’ temporal memory enable superior adaptation to non-stationary environments compared to fixed or memory-less evolving protocols, as demonstrated by significant improvements in task success and communication efficiency that degrade notably when temporal memory is ablated.

BACKGROUND:  
Effective communication in multi-agent systems (MAS) is crucial for coordination, especially under environment shifts that alter task dynamics mid-episode. Prior work has explored emergent communication and protocol evolution but often neglects the explicit role of temporal memory in leveraging sequential communication history for adaptation. Understanding whether and how temporal memory uniquely supports flexible, robust communication in dynamic, non-stationary settings remains an open challenge.

APPROACH:  
We propose training decentralized agents with deep recurrent neural networks (e.g., LSTMs) that jointly learn evolving discrete communication protocols via reinforcement learning with a Gumbel-Softmax bottleneck, enabling temporal integration of previous messages and observations. This approach is contrasted against (1) evolving protocols without recurrent memory and (2) static, handcrafted protocols following Sukhbaatar et al. (2016), with all conditions rigorously matched for model capacity, communication bandwidth, and training budget to isolate the effect of temporal memory on adaptation.

EXPERIMENT:  
Using the OpenAI Multi-Agent Particle Environment’s Cooperative Navigation and Physical Deception tasks, augmented with engineered within-episode environment shifts that alter agent roles, goals, and communication constraints, we evaluate adaptation on unseen environment variants. Metrics include average episodic reward and communication efficiency quantified via normalized message entropy and bandwidth usage. Statistical analysis across ≥5 random seeds tests for a minimum 10% relative reward improvement by temporal memory agents and a ≥15% performance drop upon ablating temporal memory.

NOVELTY:  
This work uniquely isolates the contribution of temporal memory from protocol flexibility and network size in emergent communication, providing a rigorous theoretical and empirical framework for its necessity in non-stationary MAS tasks. Unlike prior studies that focus on static or memory-less protocols, our method demonstrates that temporal dependencies in communication are critical for agents to disambiguate signals and adapt effectively to dynamically shifting environments.

topic: Emergent communication in multi-agent systems
text:
IDEA:  
Multi-agent systems that learn emergent communication protocols via adaptive, dynamically modulated network topologies will demonstrate significantly faster adaptation and improved task-switching performance compared to systems using fixed or static communication graphs, as evaluated through controlled topology interventions and rigorous baselines.

BACKGROUND:  
Effective communication is critical for coordination in multi-agent systems (MAS), yet most emergent communication research assumes static or fully connected communication topologies, limiting adaptability to changing environments or tasks. The open problem is whether enabling agents to dynamically modulate their communication topology—selectively gating connections based on state—can yield more robust, generalizable protocols that accelerate adaptation to new tasks under domain shifts. Addressing this gap promises practical advances in scalable, flexible MAS coordination.

APPROACH:  
We introduce a topology modulation network (TMN) that, at each timestep, stochastically generates sparse adjacency matrices conditioned on agent internal states, jointly optimized with policy parameters via policy gradient reinforcement learning. This dynamic topology encourages agents to develop communication strategies resilient to fluctuating neighbors and message paths while preserving communication capacity through controlled sparsity. We compare this to fixed fully connected and intermediate sparse static graphs, as well as no-communication baselines, controlling for model capacity and bandwidth.

EXPERIMENT:  
We evaluate on Multi-Agent Particle Environment (MPE) for lightweight prototyping and the StarCraft II Multi-Agent Challenge (SMAC) for complex coordination under partial observability. Agents train sequentially on distinct tasks (e.g., target collection or enemy engagement) where Task B differs qualitatively from Task A. Metrics include (a) number of episodes to reach 90% of empirically determined maximum achievable reward on Task B, validated by exhaustive single-task training runs to avoid circularity, and (b) asymptotic Task B reward after a fixed training budget. Statistical significance is established via multiple random seeds and ablation studies (e.g., frozen TMN, no communication).

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior work that assumes fixed or manually designed communication graphs or focuses solely on compositional protocol emergence, our TMN jointly learns dynamic, stochastic topologies enabling communication adaptivity and robustness. We provide a formal conceptual grounding relating topology modulation to improved representational generalization under nonstationary interaction graphs, and address training stability challenges through variance reduction, regularization, and curriculum learning, establishing the first controlled experimental evidence that dynamic communication topologies enhance adaptation speed in MAS.

topic: Emergent communication in multi-agent systems
text:
IDEA:  
Multi-agent systems equipped with heterogeneous sensory modalities (visual, proprioceptive, and auditory) develop more robust and informative emergent communication protocols under noisy environmental conditions compared to systems relying on homogeneous sensory inputs.

BACKGROUND:  
Emergent communication in cooperative multi-agent systems (MAS) often relies on homogeneous sensory inputs, limiting robustness when sensory data is corrupted by noise. Real-world MAS operate in noisy, uncertain environments where integrating multiple sensory modalities could enhance communication resilience and task performance. However, theoretical understanding and empirical validation of how sensory heterogeneity affects emergent communication robustness remain underexplored.

APPROACH:  
We design a modular multi-encoder neural architecture where each sensory modality (CNN for vision, MLP for proprioception, RNN for auditory signals) is processed independently before fusion into a shared latent representation that passes through a discrete communication bottleneck using Gumbel-Softmax relaxation. Agents are trained end-to-end in a differentiable sender-receiver framework with joint reinforcement learning objectives on cooperative signaling tasks in the Multi-Agent Particle Environment extended with multimodal inputs (MPE-MultiModal). Noise with controlled Signal-to-Noise Ratios (20dB to 0dB Gaussian noise) is injected consistently across sensory channels during training and evaluation to simulate environmental unreliability.

EXPERIMENT:  
We compare heterogeneous input agents (visual + proprioceptive + auditory) against homogeneous input agents (single modality only) using the standardized MPE-MultiModal dataset (Wang et al., 2022) on target-location signaling tasks. Metrics include task completion accuracy, mutual information of discrete communication symbols estimated with bias-corrected methods, and robustness quantified by accuracy degradation slopes across noise levels. Statistical evaluation uses paired t-tests with 30 independent runs, reporting effect sizes and confidence intervals. Baselines include (a) standard MPE communication with visual inputs only and (b) the template transfer emergent communication method (2019).

NOVELTY:  
This work establishes a theoretically motivated and empirically validated link between sensory heterogeneity and emergent communication robustness in MAS, distinguishing itself through (1) integration and synchronization of multimodal sensory inputs in MPE, (2) rigorous noise injection protocols and ablations controlling for architectural capacity, and (3) robust statistical analysis of communication informativeness and task performance under noise—advancing beyond prior homogeneous-input emergent communication studies and developmentally motivated compositional methods.

topic: Emergent communication in multi-agent systems
text:
IDEA:  
Agents trained under dynamically changing task objectives in multi-agent communication systems develop more compositional emergent languages than those trained on static tasks, as measured by rigorously validated compositionality metrics.

BACKGROUND:  
Emergent communication in multi-agent systems often relies on fixed, static task objectives, limiting the natural development of compositional languages. It remains an open question whether introducing task dynamism—where objectives shift contextually during interaction—can causally induce more compositional communication protocols. Existing work typically conflates task dynamism with multi-turn dialog complexity or dataset-specific biases, leaving the specific impact of dynamic objectives on compositionality underexplored.

APPROACH:  
We implement a sender-receiver architecture with a discrete communication channel trained via the Gumbel-Softmax trick combined with reinforcement learning, augmented by modular attention heads explicitly biasing compositionality. To isolate the effect of task dynamism, we introduce controlled experimental conditions including (a) static multi-turn tasks, (b) dynamic single-turn tasks, and (c) fully dynamic multi-turn tasks, all based on adaptations of the CLEVR and CLEVR-Dialog datasets. Compositionality is assessed using validated metrics—topographic similarity, BLEU adapted for emergent languages, and additional metrics such as the Mutual Information Gap—to triangulate and robustly quantify compositional structure.

EXPERIMENT:  
We compare agents trained on (1) static CLEVR single-turn tasks, (2) static CLEVR multi-turn tasks with fixed objectives, (3) dynamic CLEVR single-turn tasks with changing objectives, and (4) dynamic CLEVR-Dialog multi-turn tasks. Baselines include continuous communication channels and the obverter algorithm on matched datasets. Significance testing (p < 0.01) on improvements in compositionality metrics coupled with maintained task accuracy (>90%) will validate the hypothesis; failure to observe improvements or task accuracy trade-offs (<80%) will falsify it.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior work that conflates dialog complexity with task dynamism or relies on architectural biases without controlling for confounds, this study rigorously disentangles task dynamism as a causal factor for compositional language emergence. It further strengthens metric validation and feasibility by integrating controlled experimental conditions and modular inductive biases, providing new theoretical insight into how dynamic environments foster compositional communication in multi-agent systems.

topic: Causal discovery from observational data
text:
IDEA:  
Incorporating domain-specific causal constraints derived from expert knowledge into nonlinear, high-dimensional time series causal discovery algorithms significantly improves the accuracy and robustness of inferred causal graphs compared to purely data-driven approaches.

BACKGROUND:  
Causal discovery from observational time series data remains challenging in complex nonlinear, high-dimensional systems due to limited samples, latent confounding, and the difficulty of reliably estimating causal directions. Existing state-of-the-art methods often rely solely on data-driven conditional independence tests or deep learning architectures, which can produce spurious or ambiguous causal links without leveraging available domain expertise. Integrating expert-derived causal constraints offers a promising yet underexplored avenue to enhance the identifiability and interpretability of causal models in such settings.

APPROACH:  
We propose augmenting leading nonlinear causal discovery algorithms—PCMCI+ and TCDF—by encoding domain-specific constraints as hard or soft priors during causal graph search, pruning, or edge scoring. These constraints, grounded in expert knowledge from two benchmark datasets (the CAMELS Earth system climate dataset and the CHB-MIT Scalp EEG biomedical dataset), will forbid implausible edges and enforce known causal directions, implemented as adjacency masks or penalty terms integrated into conditional independence tests and attention mechanisms. Rigorous sensitivity analyses will be conducted by systematically varying the completeness and correctness of these constraints to assess robustness.

EXPERIMENT:  
The approach will be evaluated on the CAMELS and CHB-MIT EEG datasets using Structural Hamming Distance (SHD) and F1-score against expert-validated ground-truth causal graphs as metrics. Baselines include PCMCI+, TCDF, and CAnDOIT (in observational mode). Statistical significance of improvements will be established via bootstrapped confidence intervals, with additional tests assessing robustness to reduced sample size and added noise. Ablation studies with randomized or perturbed domain constraints will isolate the effect of expert knowledge integration.

NOVELTY:  
This work provides a principled and scalable framework for integrating domain causal constraints into both classical nonlinear conditional independence-based and deep learning-based causal discovery methods, backed by theoretical analysis of identifiability and constraint interaction in nonlinear time series. By explicitly quantifying the impact and robustness of expert knowledge in high-dimensional, noisy scenarios, it moves beyond purely data-driven models and existing constraint-based approaches that lack comprehensive evaluation in such complex settings.

topic: Causal discovery from observational data
text:
IDEA: Integrating domain-specific symbolic knowledge as differentiable constraints into neural causal discovery models enhances the accuracy and robustness of causal graph recovery from nonlinear observational time series compared to purely data-driven methods.

BACKGROUND: Causal discovery from nonlinear observational time series remains challenging due to complexity, limited samples, and high dimensionality, often resulting in inaccurate or unstable causal graphs. While neural methods like TCDF demonstrate strong data-driven performance, they typically ignore valuable domain knowledge that could guide learning and prevent implausible causal inferences. Effectively incorporating symbolic domain knowledge into neural causal discovery models holds promise but lacks systematic validation and theoretical grounding.

APPROACH: We propose a hybrid causal discovery framework extending TCDF by integrating domain-specific symbolic knowledge via a differentiable loss term that penalizes violations of symbolic causal constraints (e.g., temporal precedence, forbidden edges) encoded as relaxed logical rules. The method trains end-to-end on nonlinear time series data with a tunable hyperparameter controlling the trade-off between data fitting and constraint adherence. Comprehensive ablation studies vary constraint strength and fidelity, including tests with noisy or incorrect symbolic knowledge, to validate robustness and isolate the impact of domain knowledge integration.

EXPERIMENT: We evaluate our method on three benchmark datasets with known ground truth causal graphs and domain knowledge: (1) Lorenz-96 chaotic dynamical system; (2) PhysioNet Challenge 2012 ICU multivariate physiological time series with expert-curated causal relations; and (3) synthetic nonlinear gene regulatory networks generated from biologically plausible ODE models. Baselines include TCDF, PCMCI+, and Neural Granger Causality. Performance is quantified by Structural Hamming Distance (SHD) and F1-score, with statistical significance assessed via paired bootstrap tests. Success requires ≥10% relative SHD reduction and ≥5 percentage point F1 improvement over the best baseline, while failure to improve beyond ±2% or p≥0.1 falsifies the hypothesis.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior work that is purely data-driven or heuristically incorporates prior knowledge, our approach formalizes domain knowledge as differentiable symbolic constraints embedded directly into neural causal discovery training, enabling principled, end-to-end learning with explicit trade-offs. This systematic integration and rigorous validation on diverse nonlinear time series benchmarks represent a novel methodological and empirical contribution to causal discovery literature.

topic: Causal discovery from observational data
text:
IDEA: Integrating domain-specific symbolic constraints as a regularized projection within deep learning-based temporal causal discovery frameworks improves the accuracy and reliability of causal graph recovery from nonlinear time series data compared to purely data-driven methods.

BACKGROUND: Accurately inferring causal relationships from high-dimensional nonlinear time series remains a fundamental challenge due to model identifiability, limited samples, and complex dynamical dependencies. Existing deep learning causal discovery methods like TCDF excel in capturing nonlinearities but often ignore valuable domain knowledge, while constraint-free methods risk implausible or spurious causal structures. Incorporating domain-specific symbolic constraints promises to guide learning toward more accurate and interpretable causal graphs, yet their practical impact and theoretical guarantees remain underexplored.

APPROACH: We propose extending TCDF by embedding domain-specific symbolic constraints—expressed as logic rules or adjacency masks encoding prior causal knowledge—as a regularization term in the loss function and as a projection step on the learned adjacency matrix during training. This hybrid method balances prediction accuracy, graph sparsity, and symbolic consistency, with ablation studies varying constraint correctness and strength to robustly quantify their influence under realistic noise and uncertainty. We explicitly analyze assumptions regarding constraint validity and identifiability, and develop scalable optimization strategies ensuring efficient convergence without excessive overhead.

EXPERIMENT: We will evaluate the hybrid method against TCDF, PCMCI+, and CAnDOIT on three datasets: (1) the Human Connectome Project fMRI data with anatomical connectivity constraints, (2) CMIP6 climate model time series with physical causal constraints, and (3) synthetic nonlinear dynamical systems (e.g., Lorenz-96) with injected noisy symbolic constraints. Performance will be assessed via Structural Hamming Distance, Precision, Recall, and F1 score, with paired statistical tests; success requires at least 15% relative SHD reduction and 10% F1 improvement over TCDF across datasets, including ablations isolating constraint impact.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior work that applies purely data-driven deep learning or minimally incorporates domain knowledge, this approach systematically integrates symbolic causal constraints directly into the TCDF’s learning objective and projection step, providing explicit theoretical framing, robustness analyses under constraint noise, and scalable optimization methods—thereby advancing both the theoretical understanding and empirical performance of causal discovery in nonlinear time series.

topic: Causal discovery from observational data
text:
IDEA: Incorporating domain-specific causal constraints derived from expert knowledge as hard or soft priors into nonlinear time series causal discovery algorithms significantly reduces false positive causal edges and structural errors without compromising recall.

BACKGROUND: Causal discovery from high-dimensional, nonlinear observational time series is challenged by spurious causal links and false positives due to complex dynamics and limited identifiability. While purely data-driven methods like TCDF, PCMCI+, and CAnDOIT achieve state-of-the-art performance, they often produce false positives that contradict known domain principles. Integrating expert knowledge as causal constraints has been proposed but lacks systematic evaluation on realistic nonlinear time series domains and rigorous theoretical justification.

APPROACH: We formalize domain knowledge as edge presence and direction constraints encoded as masks or priors, and extend TCDF and PCMCI+ to enforce these constraints during graph search and edge pruning—e.g., by disallowing forbidden edges in attention mechanisms or conditioning sets and applying penalties in loss functions. We conduct extensive ablation studies comparing hard versus soft constraints and partial versus complete domain knowledge, testing robustness to constraint misspecification. To validate, we include experiments on synthetic datasets with fully known ground truth alongside real-world high-dimensional nonlinear time series from the Human Connectome Project (resting-state fMRI with anatomical connectivity constraints) and ERA5 climate reanalysis (atmospheric variables with physical causality rules).

EXPERIMENT: We evaluate false positive rate (FPR), precision, recall, F1 score, and Structural Hamming Distance (SHD) against expert-validated anatomical and physical causal graphs, comparing baseline unconstrained TCDF, PCMCI+, and CAnDOIT with their constrained extensions. Statistical significance will be assessed to confirm a minimum 15% relative reduction in FPR and SHD without more than 5% recall loss; the hypothesis is falsified if constraints fail to improve or harm performance beyond baseline variance or cause >10% recall drop.

NOVELTY: This work rigorously quantifies the impact of domain-specific causal constraints on nonlinear time series causal discovery, providing the first integrated framework combining deep learning and constraint-based methods with formalized domain priors and robustness analyses. It uniquely pairs theoretical insights on identifiability improvements with extensive synthetic and real-data validation, differentiating it from prior heuristic or purely data-driven approaches.

topic: Causal discovery from observational data
text:
IDEA:  
Incorporating explicitly learned causal invariances across multiple related nonlinear observational time series datasets improves the robustness and accuracy of causal graph recovery compared to single-dataset and naive multi-dataset methods.

BACKGROUND:  
Causal discovery from nonlinear, high-dimensional observational time series is a critical challenge in domains like climate science, physiology, and finance, where underlying causal mechanisms may be shared but obscured by domain-specific nonlinearities and noise. Existing methods either focus on single datasets or naively pool heterogeneous data, often resulting in unstable or inaccurate causal graphs. Leveraging invariant causal relations across related datasets holds promise but lacks thorough validation and theoretical grounding in nonlinear time series contexts.

APPROACH:  
We propose Multi-Dataset Invariant Causal Discovery (MD-ICD), extending Temporal Causal Discovery Framework (TCDF) by introducing a shared causal graph prior and dataset-specific neural feature extractors. MD-ICD jointly trains across datasets with an invariance regularizer that penalizes variability in causal edges, explicitly enforcing the discovery of causal mechanisms consistent across datasets while allowing for dataset-specific nonlinear transformations and noise. Intermediate baselines including multi-dataset TCDF without invariance penalties and random invariance constraints will isolate the effect of the invariance regularizer.

EXPERIMENT:  
Experiments will be conducted on carefully selected, domain-aligned datasets with partially known causal relations: (1) ERA5 reanalysis climate variables (temperature, humidity, pressure) from geographically distinct but climatologically related regions; (2) PhysioNet ICU patient vitals data across multiple hospitals with overlapping measurement protocols; and (3) minute-level stock indices data from S&P500 and FTSE100 markets during overlapping time periods. We will evaluate causal graph recovery accuracy using precision, recall, and F1-score against held-out ground truth or expert-validated proxy causal relations and measure graph stability under data perturbations. Statistical significance will be tested with paired tests, requiring MD-ICD to outperform best single-dataset TCDF and naive pooling baselines by at least 5% absolute F1-score improvement with p < 0.01.

NOVELTY:  
MD-ICD is the first approach to integrate deep nonlinear causal discovery with an explicit invariance regularizer across multiple heterogeneous time series datasets, supported by theoretical assumptions on identifiability and robustness to partial invariance violations. Unlike prior works focusing on single datasets or naive pooling, MD-ICD models dataset-specific nonlinearities while discovering shared causal structures, enabling more robust and interpretable causal inference in real-world complex dynamical systems.

topic: Mechanistic interpretability of transformer models
text:
IDEA:  
Interpretability of transformer models varies nonlinearly with depth, peaking in the middle layers where mechanistically decipherable circuits are most reliably discovered and quantitatively validated.

BACKGROUND:  
While mechanistic interpretability aims to reverse-engineer neural circuits underlying transformer behavior, it remains unclear how interpretability is distributed across layers. Prior work often focuses on isolated layers or entire models without systematically quantifying layerwise interpretability, leaving open whether mid-level layers encode more coherent, causally influential circuits than early or late layers. Addressing this gap is crucial for understanding hierarchical computation and guiding circuit discovery efforts.

APPROACH:  
We propose an automated, layerwise circuit discovery pipeline applied to GPT-2 small, integrating activation patching, causal mediation analysis, and attention-MLP interaction graphs to identify and validate mechanistic circuits per layer. Objective, pre-registered metrics—circuit discovery success rate (fraction of circuits exceeding fidelity thresholds), behavior coverage, and interpretability coherence—are computed with robust controls including random and cross-layer ablations to isolate genuine circuit contributions.

EXPERIMENT:  
We test the hypothesis by applying the pipeline across all 12 transformer layers on two diverse benchmark datasets—the Big-Bench Hard (BBH) reasoning subset and Mechanical Turk semantic probe tasks—measuring nonlinear trends in circuit discovery success rates and statistical significance assessed by bootstrapped confidence intervals and blinded evaluation.

NOVELTY:  
This work rigorously quantifies layerwise mechanistic interpretability with an automated, scalable methodology, explicitly testing for a nonlinear, mid-layer peak in circuit fidelity across multiple tasks, thus advancing beyond prior single-layer or ad hoc studies and providing a theoretically motivated framework to explain layerwise interpretability variation in transformer models.

topic: Mechanistic interpretability of transformer models
text:
IDEA:  
Systematically quantify the graded, distributed contributions of transformer attention heads and feedforward submodules to model behavior using statistically rigorous ablation and attribution techniques, to test whether mechanistic circuits are overlapping and entangled or modular and independently removable.

BACKGROUND:  
Mechanistic interpretability seeks to reverse-engineer transformer models by identifying internal subcircuits responsible for distinct functions, but existing work often assumes a simplistic one-head–one-subcircuit modularity which neglects the likely distributed and overlapping nature of neural computations. Current ablation studies largely rely on binary, threshold-driven interpretations without formal statistical grounding, limiting insights into the causal roles and interdependence of transformer components. A refined understanding of mechanistic modularity that accounts for graded dependencies and distributed circuits is necessary to advance interpretability theory and practical model analysis.

APPROACH:  
We propose a comprehensive ablation framework on GPT-2 Medium that simultaneously examines single-head, multi-head, and feedforward module perturbations, leveraging attention attribution scores derived via stability-verified causal attribution methods on large validation sets. Ablation effects will be analyzed using repeated trials to estimate confidence intervals and effect size distributions rather than fixed cutoffs, enabling a continuous, statistically principled characterization of component importance and redundancy. Complementary noise injection controls will differentiate specific ablation effects from general perturbation sensitivity, thus refining causal inference.

EXPERIMENT:  
Performance impact of targeted ablations will be evaluated on three linguistically and cognitively diverse benchmarks—LAMBADA (contextual understanding), HellaSwag (commonsense reasoning), and BBH subset (arithmetic and logic)—using task-appropriate accuracy and perplexity metrics. Statistical significance of performance degradation relative to baseline and noise controls will be assessed across multiple runs to test hypotheses about independence versus entanglement of subcircuits.

NOVELTY:  
This work advances mechanistic interpretability by moving beyond binary, one-head-centric ablations to a graded, statistically grounded framework that incorporates feedforward modules and noise controls, aligning with recent insights on distributed and overlapping circuit architectures. Unlike prior studies, it quantifies causal contributions continuously and rigorously, providing new theoretical clarity and practical methodology for disentangling the entangled mechanistic substrates in transformer models.

topic: Mechanistic interpretability of transformer models
text:
IDEA:  
Investigate whether specific attention heads in pretrained multilingual transformer models encode algorithmically interpretable syntactic parsing subroutines that reliably generalize across typologically diverse languages, by quantifying their syntactic role alignment and probing performance relative to rigorous multilingual baselines.

BACKGROUND:  
While transformer attention has been empirically linked to syntactic structure, it remains unclear if individual attention heads implement discrete, reusable algorithmic subroutines for parsing that extend beyond language-specific idiosyncrasies. Prior work often conflates correlation with mechanistic interpretability and lacks robust cross-lingual evaluation controlling for confounds such as token frequency and sentence structure. Establishing if and how syntactic information is mechanistically encoded in attention heads across languages with divergent grammar is a key open problem in understanding transformer internals.

APPROACH:  
We propose a controlled multilingual probing framework that extracts and normalizes attention weights from each head in pretrained multilingual transformers (mBERT, XLM-R) and compares them to gold-standard dependency parses from typologically distinct languages (English, Finnish, Japanese) in the Universal Dependencies corpus. We compute refined attention-to-syntactic-role alignment metrics corrected for positional and frequency biases, and train both linear and nonlinear probes on attention-derived features to predict dependency labels, benchmarking against randomly initialized and monolingual BERT baselines to isolate syntactic signal.

EXPERIMENT:  
Using UD test sets for English, Finnish, and Japanese, we evaluate (1) normalized attention alignment scores quantifying how strongly each head attends to syntactic dependents, and (2) syntactic probing accuracy from classifiers trained on frozen attention features, assessing statistical significance via paired permutation tests. The hypothesis is falsified if no attention head consistently outperforms baselines across all languages, or if high-performing heads fail to demonstrate cross-lingual generalization.

NOVELTY:  
This study advances mechanistic interpretability by explicitly operationalizing and normalizing attention-syntax alignment as a cross-lingual, algorithmic subroutine hypothesis—moving beyond prior correlational analyses and monolingual probing work—and rigorously benchmarking against strong baselines and nonlinear probes to disentangle genuine syntactic computation from confounds, thereby providing clearer mechanistic insight into transformer attention heads across diverse grammar systems.

topic: Mechanistic interpretability of transformer models
text:
IDEA:  
Systematically identify and validate whether specific transformer attention heads implement stable, discrete symbolic operations that causally govern multi-step reasoning, using rigorously defined attribution, intervention, and interpretability metrics across diverse structured reasoning tasks.

BACKGROUND:  
While mechanistic interpretability aims to reverse-engineer transformer computations, the extent to which discrete symbolic operations localize to individual attention heads remains unresolved. Prior studies often rely on anecdotal or qualitative evidence that single heads correspond to interpretable functions, but emerging findings suggest reasoning may be distributed or entangled across multiple components. A rigorous, falsifiable framework with quantitative controls is needed to clarify the granularity and stability of symbolic computations in transformers.

APPROACH:  
We combine validated attribution methods (attention roll-out, integrated gradients) with ground-truth synthetic benchmarks to reliably identify candidate heads linked to discrete symbolic reasoning steps. Using activation patching and targeted head ablations, we causally test if manipulating these heads predictably flips intermediate reasoning states, operationalized through a formal consistency score. Symbolic interpretability is quantified by training symbolic classifiers on head activations to decode discrete reasoning operations with calibrated fidelity thresholds, ensuring robust, reproducible identification of interpretable heads.

EXPERIMENT:  
The evaluation spans two structured reasoning datasets—CLUTRR (family relation logical inference) and GSM8K (multi-step arithmetic problems)—fine-tuning GPT-2 medium and comparing against randomly initialized transformers as controls. Key metrics include (a) consistency score measuring how often single-head interventions flip targeted reasoning steps (>75% success threshold), (b) task accuracy deltas post-intervention (>15% drop indicating criticality), and (c) symbolic classifier fidelity (>80% accuracy for interpretability). Comprehensive controls include interventions on irrelevant or random heads and pretrained-but-non-finetuned models. The hypothesis is falsified if no heads meet both interpretability and causal control criteria across datasets.

NOVELTY:  
This work advances mechanistic interpretability by establishing a rigorous, cross-dataset quantitative framework that integrates validated head identification, precise behavioral metrics, and strong causal interventions—moving beyond anecdotal evidence to systematically test and potentially falsify the localization of symbolic reasoning operations to individual transformer heads.

topic: Mechanistic interpretability of transformer models
text:
IDEA:  
Systematically evaluate whether individual attention heads in transformer models encode consistent, distinct algorithmic subroutines corresponding to human-interpretable symbolic manipulations across multiple algorithmically structured datasets, while explicitly testing for distributed and overlapping functional representations.

BACKGROUND:  
Mechanistic interpretability seeks to reverse-engineer the internal computations of transformer models to understand how they represent symbolic and algorithmic functions. Prior work often assumes localized functional roles for single attention heads but lacks rigorous cross-task validation and may overlook distributed or mixed representations. This raises the open question of whether any attention head reliably implements distinct symbolic operations consistently across datasets, or if these functions are diffusely encoded.

APPROACH:  
We propose a rigorous, multi-dataset intervention framework combining causal mediation analysis and activation patching to quantify the functional contribution of individual heads with a principled Functional Attribution Score (FAS), augmented by information-theoretic and layer-wise relevance metrics. By correlating head activations with interpretable symbolic features and testing causal effects of targeted activations on model outputs, we will assess both localized and distributed representations, incorporating rigorous controls such as sham patching and distribution-shift tests to ensure causal validity.

EXPERIMENT:  
We analyze pretrained transformer models (GPT-2 medium and a smaller Transformer trained from scratch) on three algorithmically rich datasets: ListOps (nested list operations), PCFG formal grammar parsing, and the BIG-Bench Induction task. Baselines include random head ablations and distributed encoding models from prior literature. We identify candidate heads via symbolic feature correlations and measure their FAS—defined as normalized task performance drops upon ablation—requiring >10% FAS on ≥2 related datasets to claim replicable specialization. Failure to observe consistent FAS or reproducible feature correlations falsifies the hypothesis.

NOVELTY:  
This work uniquely advances mechanistic interpretability by explicitly evaluating cross-dataset functional consistency of attention heads, integrating rigorous causal metrics and controls to distinguish localized versus distributed symbolic computations, thereby moving beyond single-task reverse-engineering to produce generalizable insights into transformer algorithmic representations.

topic: Quantum advantage in machine learning tasks
text:
IDEA:  
Quantum neural networks trained on classically intractable quantum-generated data distributions achieve statistically significant lower generalization error than classical neural networks of comparable parameter count, demonstrating quantum advantage in learning tasks beyond classical reach.

BACKGROUND:  
Demonstrating practical quantum advantage in machine learning remains an open challenge, especially when data distributions are classically hard to sample or model efficiently. Prior work has shown quantum generative models can approximate certain quantum distributions, but robust empirical evidence that quantum models outperform classical counterparts on such tasks—under fair and noise-aware conditions with rigorous evaluation metrics—has yet to be established. This research addresses whether QNNs can leverage quantum data complexity to surpass classical models in generalization performance, accounting for realistic hardware limitations.

APPROACH:  
We train parameterized variational quantum circuits (QNNs) with noise-aware error mitigation and adaptive hybrid optimization on datasets sampled from classically intractable quantum circuits, such as Google's Sycamore random circuit outputs and IQP circuit distributions. Classical baselines include (1) feedforward neural networks and (2) generative models (GANs or VAEs) with matched parameter counts and training data. Evaluation uses sample-based metrics like maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) and KL divergence where tractable, complemented by classification accuracy on cluster-labeled data, ensuring theoretical grounding linking classical sampling hardness to learning complexity.

EXPERIMENT:  
Models are trained and evaluated on identical held-out test samples from quantum-generated distributions, using paired bootstrap hypothesis testing (p < 0.05) over multiple random initializations to verify if QNNs achieve statistically significant lower MMD or KL divergence than classical models. Ablations include training classical models with artificially injected noise and testing QNNs on classically tractable data to isolate quantum advantage. Noise mitigation strategies and QNN scalability constraints are explicitly benchmarked to assess practical feasibility.

NOVELTY:  
This work advances beyond prior demonstrations of quantum generative models by rigorously integrating noise-aware training protocols, theoretically justified complexity measures linking classical hardness to learning difficulty, and comprehensive controls to isolate genuine quantum advantage in generalization performance. It provides the first experimentally and statistically robust framework for validating quantum advantage in machine learning tasks on near-term quantum devices with classically intractable data.

topic: Quantum advantage in machine learning tasks
text:
IDEA:  
Training variational quantum classifiers on near-term devices using noise-aware optimization algorithms that periodically update noise profiles significantly improves classification accuracy and robustness under slowly varying noise, but this advantage diminishes or reverses when noise fluctuates rapidly or non-stationarily.

BACKGROUND:  
Near-term quantum devices suffer from time-dependent noise that can degrade quantum machine learning model performance. Existing QML training approaches often assume static or average noise parameters, ignoring noise dynamics that affect optimization convergence and generalization. A principled understanding and exploitation of noise temporal structure to enhance training robustness and predictive accuracy remains an open challenge.

APPROACH:  
We propose a noise-aware training protocol for variational quantum classifiers that incorporates periodically updated noise characterizations—derived via low-overhead tomography or device calibration—into noise-adapted cost functions and gradient estimators. By alternating between noise profile estimation and parameter updates, the method dynamically adapts to slowly varying noise, improving gradient fidelity and mitigating error accumulation during training.

EXPERIMENT:  
We evaluate the approach on binary classification tasks using subsets of MNIST (digits 0 vs. 1) and Fashion-MNIST (T-shirts vs. pullovers) datasets, benchmarked on superconducting quantum simulators and/or hardware with realistic noise channels parameterized from device calibrations. We compare noise-aware optimization—updating noise parameters every 10 epochs—with noise-agnostic training assuming static noise, and classical SVM baselines. Metrics include test accuracy and variance across multiple training runs under engineered noise regimes with slow versus rapid noise fluctuations.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior QML works focusing on static or average noise models, this research rigorously formalizes the impact of noise temporal dynamics on training, integrates real-time noise estimation into gradient computations, and experimentally isolates the conditions under which noise-aware adaptation yields a statistically significant advantage or conversely fails, providing actionable insights into effective noise management strategies for near-term quantum machine learning.

topic: Quantum advantage in machine learning tasks
text:
IDEA:  
Demonstrate that parameterized quantum circuit classifiers implemented on 10-15 qubit NISQ devices can achieve statistically significant (>5%) superior generalization accuracy over classical kernel SVMs and neural networks on learning tasks with exponentially large quantum feature spaces, under rigorously matched training data and computational resource constraints.

BACKGROUND:  
Despite theoretical indications that quantum machine learning (QML) can exploit exponentially large Hilbert spaces to enhance learning, it remains unresolved whether NISQ-era quantum models can realize practical advantage over classical models given realistic noise and limited qubit counts. Prior works often lack strict resource parity or fail to isolate genuine quantum effects from classical analogues, leaving the question of quantum advantage on real-world or structured quantum-derived data open.

APPROACH:  
We will implement PQC classifiers using hardware-efficient and problem-inspired quantum feature maps (e.g., QAOA-style kernels) on trapped-ion or superconducting NISQ devices with 10-15 qubits, employing advanced error mitigation and noise modeling to ensure trainability. Classical baselines include kernel SVMs with RBF, polynomial, and quantum-kernel-inspired embeddings, as well as multi-layer perceptrons matched in parameter count and training budget, with additional controls using classical random feature maps designed to simulate quantum embeddings.

EXPERIMENT:  
Using Google Quantum AI’s QDATA (synthetic quantum states embedded in exponentially large Hilbert spaces) and the MNIST-Quantum-Encoded dataset (classical digits encoded via quantum feature maps), we will train all models on identical training splits (e.g., 10,000 for QDATA, 60,000 for MNIST) and cap total training time to approximate quantum device runtime plus classical optimization overhead. Performance will be measured by test accuracy and generalization gap, with quantum advantage declared if quantum models exceed classical test accuracy by ≥5% with p < 0.01 significance via bootstrap resampling.

NOVELTY:  
This work rigorously enforces resource parity, incorporates detailed noise-aware error mitigation strategies, and introduces classical controls trained on simulated quantum feature embeddings and random feature maps to isolate genuine quantum advantage. It explicitly connects data hardness assumptions and quantum kernel theoretical bounds with empirical results on real quantum hardware, surpassing prior demonstrations that lacked such comprehensive benchmarking and practical validation.

topic: Quantum advantage in machine learning tasks
text:
IDEA:  
Quantum machine learning models trained on rigorously validated synthetic datasets with genuine quantum entanglement in feature correlations achieve statistically significant improvements in generalization error over classical models—an advantage that vanishes when trained on matched datasets lacking quantum correlations.

BACKGROUND:  
Establishing a practical quantum advantage in supervised learning remains an open problem, particularly disentangling whether quantum data structure or quantum model expressivity drives performance gains. While prior works explore quantum kernels and data encoding, they often lack rigorous controls isolating entanglement as the causal factor. Demonstrating that entanglement-induced correlations in data fundamentally improve learning beyond classical capabilities is necessary to validate the promise of quantum-enhanced machine learning.

APPROACH:  
We generate paired synthetic datasets with identical classical marginal statistics but distinct quantum correlations by measuring parameterized 4-qubit entangled states versus classical analogs constructed via maximum entropy modeling preserving marginals without entanglement. A variational quantum classifier with hardware-efficient ansatz and angle encoding is trained alongside classical baselines—deep neural networks, Gaussian kernel SVMs, and boosted decision trees—matched by parameter count. We perform ablation studies removing entangling gates and incorporate noise models and error mitigation to assess robustness. Statistical tests and quantum state tomography certify dataset properties, ensuring entanglement is the only varying factor.

EXPERIMENT:  
The models are evaluated on held-out test sets using cross-entropy loss and classification accuracy with statistical significance assessed by paired t-tests (p < 0.01) and non-overlapping 95% confidence intervals over multiple random seeds. Quantum advantage is confirmed if the quantum model significantly outperforms all classical baselines on entangled data but not on non-entangled data, falsifying the hypothesis otherwise.

NOVELTY:  
This work uniquely combines rigorous quantum state certification with matched classical distribution controls to isolate entanglement’s role in learning, providing a theoretically motivated and empirically validated experimental framework beyond prior quantum kernel or generative model studies. It advances foundational understanding by explicitly linking quantum correlations in data to generalization improvements, addressing scalability and noise to demonstrate near-term feasibility.

topic: Quantum advantage in machine learning tasks
text:
IDEA:  
Quantum machine learning models employing scalable, noise-preserving feature encoding achieve statistically significant lower generalization error than optimized classical models on noisy classical datasets when the data dimension exceeds a theoretically justified threshold proportional to the number of qubits used.

BACKGROUND:  
Demonstrating a practical quantum advantage in supervised learning remains an open challenge, especially when training on classical datasets corrupted by realistic structured noise. Prior work has largely focused on asymptotic bounds or specific quantum architectures without rigorously connecting data dimensionality, noise structure, and qubit resources to generalization performance. Clarifying these relationships and establishing concrete regimes where quantum models outperform classical ones can advance understanding of QML’s practical potential under near-term hardware constraints.

APPROACH:  
We theoretically derive and experimentally validate a linear scaling law linking effective data dimensionality with the number of qubits via PQC expressivity bounds, employing a hybrid encoding strategy combining amplitude and repeated angle encoding to preserve structured noise correlations without excessive circuit depth. Quantum models are implemented as variational quantum classifiers with hardware-efficient ansätze on 4–16 qubits, trained using hybrid quantum-classical optimization. Classical baselines include extensively hyperparameter-tuned SVMs with RBF kernels and MLPs, trained with identical noise-injected datasets and dimensionality reductions.

EXPERIMENT:  
Using Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets augmented with class-dependent correlated Gaussian noise, we systematically vary data dimension via PCA from 10 up to the full feature space; then train and evaluate models using repeated randomized train-test splits and noise realizations. The primary metric is test set classification accuracy averaged over runs, with quantum advantage defined as ≥3% improvement over the best classical baseline sustained beyond a dimension threshold *k × n_qubits* (where *k* is empirically calibrated). Statistical significance is assessed by paired t-tests at 95% confidence. Ablation studies include noise-free controls and noise-only baselines to isolate effects.

NOVELTY:  
This work rigorously links PQC capacity and data dimensionality through theoretical bounds, implements a practical, noise-preserving encoding that scales with qubit count, and conducts exhaustive baseline optimization with controlled noise injection—differentiating it from prior studies that either lack theoretical dimensionality justification, neglect structured noise effects, or rely on limited baselines and hardware demonstrations without systematic scaling analyses.

topic: Scaling laws for Large Language Models
text:
IDEA:  
Investigate whether continual pretraining on mixed-domain corpora reduces the scaling exponent α that governs the power-law relationship between model size and downstream task performance, compared to single-domain or general-domain continual pretraining.

BACKGROUND:  
Scaling laws for large language models (LLMs) describe predictable improvements in performance as model size increases, but how domain-specific continual pretraining (CPT) affects these laws remains understudied. Prior work has characterized scaling in general and single-domain CPT settings, yet the impact of mixed-domain CPT—where models are continually pretrained on diverse specialized corpora simultaneously—on scaling efficiency and returns is an open problem with practical ramifications for model adaptation strategies.

APPROACH:  
Starting from a strong general-domain pretrained checkpoint (on The Pile), conduct continual pretraining on (1) single-domain corpora (MATH, CodeParrot, PubMed), and (2) a carefully balanced mixed-domain corpus combining these three domains equally. Train models at several intermediate scales (e.g., 100M, 300M, 1B, 3B parameters) under standardized hyperparameters and compute budgets to ensure comparable convergence. Fit the scaling exponent α for each CPT regime on domain-specific downstream benchmarks (MATH, HumanEval, BioASQ) using nonlinear least squares over multiple random seeds with convergence diagnostics.

EXPERIMENT:  
Evaluate downstream task performance (accuracy or F1-score) normalized within each domain, then fit and statistically compare the scaling exponents α across regimes. The hypothesis is confirmed if α for mixed-domain continual pretraining is significantly lower (e.g., >5% decrease, p<0.05) than for single-domain or general-domain CPT, indicating diminishing scaling returns due to domain mixture. Otherwise, the hypothesis is falsified.

NOVELTY:  
This work provides the first rigorous, multi-scale empirical analysis of how mixed-domain continual pretraining influences scaling law exponents in LLMs, going beyond existing single-domain CPT studies and general scaling law characterizations. By incorporating intermediate model sizes, standardized compute budgets, and robust statistical testing, it offers new theoretical and practical insights into domain mixture effects on scaling efficiency.

topic: Scaling laws for Large Language Models
text:
IDEA:  
The optimal compute allocation for domain-specific continual pretraining of large language models shifts non-linearly with model size, deviating significantly from classical scaling law predictions derived from general-domain pretraining.

BACKGROUND:  
Classical scaling laws (Kaplan et al., 2020; Nguyen et al., 2025) provide predictable power-law relationships between model size, compute, and performance for general-domain LLM pretraining, assuming fixed training data mixtures. However, how these laws extend to domain-specific continual pretraining (CPT) remains unclear, especially when balancing domain and general corpora. Understanding whether CPT induces nonlinear shifts in optimal compute allocation is critical for efficient training in specialized domains.

APPROACH:  
We empirically investigate CPT across three model sizes (125M, 1.3B, 6B parameters), training decoder-only transformers initialized from a common checkpoint. We systematically vary the mixture ratio of domain (Mathematics dataset ~12M tokens or CodeSearchNet ~150M tokens) to general corpus (C4 ~750GB), and CPT compute budgets (10–100% of total training compute). Performance is measured via cross-entropy loss on held-out domain and general datasets, plus downstream metrics (MATH accuracy and HumanEval pass@1). Scaling curves are fit to identify nonlinearities in optimal compute allocation relative to model size, contrasting with classical scaling law predictions.

EXPERIMENT:  
We conduct a controlled grid search over mixture ratios (prioritizing 0%, 25%, 50%, 75%, 100%) and CPT compute budgets (fixed-token budgets derived from pilot studies) for each model size and domain, evaluating validation losses and downstream accuracies. Statistical tests assess whether scaling exponents for optimal CPT compute allocation differ significantly (p < 0.05) from those predicted by general scaling laws, using repeated runs and controls for domain data size and overfitting.

NOVELTY:  
This study uniquely quantifies how domain-specific CPT shifts optimal compute allocation in a model-size-dependent, nonlinear manner, explicitly contrasting with and extending beyond prior universal scaling laws and fixed-ratio CPT heuristics (e.g., D-CPT Law). It also integrates rigorous statistical controls and theoretical framing to isolate domain mixture effects from confounders, providing practical guidelines for efficient domain adaptation of LLMs.

topic: Scaling laws for Large Language Models
text:
IDEA:  
Domain-specific continual pre-training (CPT) of large language models exhibits fundamentally distinct scaling laws from general LLM pretraining, characterized by non-power-law interactions and saturation effects between model size and domain dataset size in specialized fields like medicine and law.

BACKGROUND:  
While established scaling laws for general LLM pretraining show smooth power-law relationships linking model size, dataset size, and performance, it remains unclear whether these laws hold during domain-specific CPT, where model knowledge is refined on specialized corpora. Prior work has largely assumed similar scaling behaviors or focused on heuristic mixture ratios without rigorous modeling of joint scaling effects in specialized domains. Understanding whether and how domain CPT breaks general scaling laws is critical for optimizing resource allocation in domain adaptation and continual learning.

APPROACH:  
We will systematically continual pre-train base LLMs (100M, 1B, and 10B parameters) originally trained on general corpora, using controlled mixtures of domain-specific and general data in medicine (MIMIC-III, PMC-OA) and law (EDGAR, CaseLaw). By varying dataset size (10M to 1B tokens) and domain mixture ratio (0%, 25%, 50%, 75%, 100%) with carefully tuned hyperparameters per domain/model size, we will fit flexible parametric scaling models that allow interaction and saturation terms beyond additive power laws. Residual and parameter analyses against Kaplan et al. (2020) and the Predictable Scale (2025) frameworks will quantify deviations.

EXPERIMENT:  
Performance will be evaluated on domain-specific held-out tasks—clinical concept extraction (i2b2 2010) and medical question answering (MedQA) for medicine; legal document classification (LexGLUE) and contract clause extraction for law—using accuracy, F1, and cross-entropy loss metrics. Statistical tests will identify significant departures from power-law fits (e.g., R² < 0.9 and exponent differences > 0.1), with matched complexity validation splits to control dataset heterogeneity.

NOVELTY:  
This study rigorously challenges the universality of power-law scaling by introducing mechanistically motivated, interaction-aware scaling models tailored to domain-specific CPT, unlike prior work that treats domain adaptation as parameter shifts or simple mixture tuning. It provides the first controlled empirical and theoretical framework to discern whether domain CPT scaling laws require fundamentally new formulations, delivering actionable insights for efficient domain specialization of LLMs.

topic: Scaling laws for Large Language Models
text:
IDEA:  
Investigate whether the optimal compute allocation for training Large Language Models exhibits a nonlinear shift beyond 100 billion parameters, favoring disproportionately larger dataset sizes relative to model size increases to improve performance under fixed compute budgets.

BACKGROUND:  
Current empirical scaling laws (Kaplan et al., 2020) describe smooth power-law relationships between model size, dataset size, and loss, implying predictable linear or monotonic trade-offs in compute allocation. However, these laws are primarily validated below or near the 100B parameter scale, leaving open whether a phase transition or nonlinear regime arises at extreme scales where data efficiency and model capacity interact differently. Understanding this could inform efficient training strategies for the next generation of ultra-large LLMs.

APPROACH:  
We propose controlled training of LLMs in the 100B–300B parameter range with systematically varied ratios of model size to dataset size while holding total compute (FLOPs) constant, using carefully curated and domain-consistent datasets derived from *The Pile*, C4, and OpenWebText2. Performance will be evaluated through cross-entropy loss on held-out *The Pile* test data and zero-shot downstream tasks (LAMBADA, MMLU), with repeated runs and hyperparameter controls to ensure robustness. Statistical analysis will detect nonlinear trends or phase transitions in compute allocation optimality.

EXPERIMENT:  
Train LLM variants at 100B, 150B, 200B, 250B, and 300B parameters with dataset sizes scaled from ~300B to 3T tokens, maintaining FLOPs ≈ 6 × model_params × dataset_tokens; evaluate cross-entropy loss and zero-shot accuracy on *The Pile* held-out set, LAMBADA, and MMLU benchmarks. Use ANOVA and nonlinear regression to identify statistically significant deviations from linear scaling in loss relative to model/dataset size ratios.

NOVELTY:  
This work targets the largely unexplored regime beyond 100B parameters to test for nonlinear shifts in compute allocation efficiency, moving beyond existing power-law and continual pretraining scaling laws which assume smooth monotonic improvements. By integrating rigorous dataset curation, repeated trials, and explicit statistical testing, it provides a more granular and theoretically grounded characterization of scaling behavior in ultra-large LLM training regimes.

topic: Scaling laws for Large Language Models
text:
IDEA:  
Incorporate dynamically adaptive mixture ratios of domain-specific continual pre-training data driven by normalized real-time loss gradient magnitudes to improve scaling efficiency and downstream task performance of large language models compared to fixed mixture ratios optimized by grid search.

BACKGROUND:  
Optimally mixing general-domain and domain-specific data during continual pre-training (CPT) is critical for efficiently scaling large language models (LLMs) to specialized tasks, yet current practice relies on costly grid searches over fixed mixture ratios that do not adapt to model learning dynamics. Existing scaling laws and CPT research have not fully explored leveraging real-time training signals to inform data sampling ratios, leaving open the question of whether adaptive data mixture strategies can yield better convergence and task transfer efficiency.

APPROACH:  
We propose a scalable adaptive data sampling algorithm that estimates per-dataset gradient norm magnitudes aggregated over mini-batches with exponential moving average smoothing to reduce noise and computational overhead. After fixed token intervals, the domain-specific data sampling ratio is updated proportionally to the normalized gradient magnitudes, prioritizing data contributing stronger learning signals. This dynamic ratio adjustment is integrated seamlessly within the training loop without disrupting throughput.

EXPERIMENT:  
We will pretrain transformer LLMs of varying sizes (125M to 1.3B parameters) on a mixture of *The Pile* (general corpus) and *CodeSearchNet* (code domain corpus), comparing: (a) fixed mixture ratios (e.g., 90:10, 70:30, 50:50) selected via grid search; (b) domain-only and general-only baselines; and (c) our proposed adaptive ratio method. Evaluation metrics include validation cross-entropy loss on a held-out representative mixed test set, code summarization accuracy on CodeSearchNet, out-of-domain robustness metrics, and calibration scores. We ensure matched token exposure across conditions and conduct ablations controlling for compute budget and sampling variance. The hypothesis is falsified if adaptive sampling does not yield a ≥2% reduction in loss or ≥3% absolute improvement in domain task accuracy over the best fixed-ratio baseline.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior work such as the D-CPT Law that relies on static, grid-searched mixture ratios, our method uniquely leverages normalized real-time gradient norms as a principled, theoretically motivated adaptive signal for data importance, operationalized via a computationally efficient smoothing mechanism. This combines insights from adaptive curriculum learning and multi-task optimization to provide a rigorous, scalable framework that directly links data mixture dynamics to empirical scaling laws and downstream task gains.

topic: Energy-efficient neuromorphic computing
text:
IDEA:  
Integrating ferroelectric tunnel junctions (FTJs) with memristive synapses based on Hf₀.₅Zr₀.₅O₂ barriers reduces energy consumption per synaptic event by more than 50% compared to conventional atomic layer deposited HfO₂ memristors without compromising synaptic performance.

BACKGROUND:  
Energy-efficiency remains a critical bottleneck in neuromorphic hardware, where synaptic event energy directly impacts scalability and practicality. Conventional HfO₂-based memristors offer reliable switching but have limited energy reduction potential under fixed operating conditions. Leveraging ferroelectric tunnel barriers promises non-volatile polarization switching at lower voltages, potentially enabling substantial synaptic energy savings while maintaining device endurance and retention.

APPROACH:  
We propose fabricating hybrid FTJ-memristor synapses by integrating ultrathin (~2 nm) ferroelectric Hf₀.₅Zr₀.₅O₂ tunnel barriers atop standard memristive layers in crossbar arrays, interfaced with identical CMOS neuron circuits. Rigorous theoretical modeling of ferroelectric switching dynamics will guide device design to optimize energy and reliability trade-offs, while calibrated electrical characterization with spike-shaped pulses will quantify switching energy and synaptic behavior under matched voltage, pulse width, and temperature conditions.

EXPERIMENT:  
Energy per synaptic event will be measured using on-chip calibrated current sensors and high-resolution oscilloscopes during potentiation/depression in neuromorphic arrays benchmarked on N-MNIST and DVS Gesture datasets, with offline-trained identical spiking neural network topologies mapped at equivalent weight precision. Success requires ≥50% energy reduction relative to ALD HfO₂ memristor arrays while maintaining linearity, endurance, and retention within ±10% of baseline; failure to meet these criteria will falsify the hypothesis.

NOVELTY:  
This work pioneers the direct integration of ferroelectric tunnel junctions with memristive synapses in neuromorphic hardware and couples rigorous theoretical analysis with real workload benchmarking to quantitatively prove significant energy savings beyond prior art focused solely on conventional HfO₂ memristors or emerging 2D/quantum materials, thus providing a scalable and CMOS-compatible path to ultra-low-energy neuromorphic computing.

topic: Energy-efficient neuromorphic computing
text:
IDEA: Incorporating a precisely engineered heterostructured quantum-dot (QD) layer within HfO₂-based memristive synapses reduces switching energy by at least 30% without degrading synaptic weight linearity, thereby enhancing energy efficiency for neuromorphic computing applications.

BACKGROUND: Energy-efficient memristive synapses are critical for scalable neuromorphic hardware, yet achieving substantial reductions in switching energy often comes at the cost of synaptic weight update linearity and device reliability. Current interface engineering approaches improve either energy or linearity, but rarely both simultaneously, and lack integration of quantum-dot heterostructures as an active modulation layer.

APPROACH: We will fabricate memristive devices based on atomic layer deposited HfO₂ with and without an embedded monodisperse colloidal quantum-dot heterostructure (e.g., PbS or CdSe QDs) precisely deposited between the switching layer and electrode. Electrical characterization under controlled pulsed voltage protocols will quantify energy-per-switch and analog conductance update linearity, while system-level benchmarking using a crossbar array and neuromorphic inference accelerator will evaluate functional impact on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST classification accuracy.

EXPERIMENT: We will compare QD-enhanced devices against identically fabricated baseline HfO₂ memristors and state-of-the-art ALD HfO₂ memristors from the 2020 literature (ref #4), measuring switching energy averaged over 1000 cycles (target ≥30% reduction) and synaptic weight nonlinearity (NL), requiring less than 5% degradation relative to baseline. Device-in-the-loop simulations on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST datasets will confirm classification accuracy remains within ±1% of baseline, ensuring no functional compromise.

NOVELTY: This work uniquely integrates heterostructured quantum-dot layers into conventional ALD HfO₂ memristors to actively modulate filament dynamics, leveraging quantum confinement effects to simultaneously reduce switching energy and maintain linear synaptic updates—an advancement beyond prior interface and materials engineering approaches that either lack quantum-dot integration or fail to meet combined energy and linearity targets.

topic: Energy-efficient neuromorphic computing
text:
IDEA: Integrating phase-change materials (PCMs) with memristive synapses in a hybrid device architecture reduces the average energy consumption per synaptic weight update by at least 30% compared to pure memristor-based synapses, while maintaining comparable classification accuracy on neuromorphic tasks.

BACKGROUND: Energy efficiency remains a critical bottleneck in neuromorphic computing hardware, where memristor-based synapses show promise but suffer from non-ideal weight update linearity and energy overhead. Hybrid synapses combining PCMs such as Ge₂Sb₂Te₅ with memristors offer potential to leverage low-energy phase transitions for fine-grained, energy-efficient weight modulation, yet quantitative energy savings and training efficacy under matched conditions remain unproven.

APPROACH: We propose fabricating and characterizing two synapse arrays—pure memristor-based (e.g., HfO₂ or TaOx) and hybrid PCM-memristor devices—integrated into spiking neural networks trained on the Fashion-MNIST dataset using spike-timing-dependent plasticity or surrogate gradient methods adapted for hardware constraints. Optimized electrical pulse protocols will be employed to minimize energy per weight update, with detailed physical and circuit-level energy models guiding design and ensuring fair, matched operational regimes.

EXPERIMENT: Energy per synaptic weight update will be precisely measured using high-resolution electrical instrumentation (oscilloscopes and source measurement units) across thousands of updates during training on Fashion-MNIST, with accuracy evaluated to confirm performance within 2% of the baseline memristor network. The hypothesis will be falsified if energy savings are below 30% or if accuracy degrades beyond this threshold.

NOVELTY: This work rigorously quantifies energy savings of hybrid PCM-memristor synapses with comprehensive physical modeling, matched workload calibration, and statistically validated device fabrication, differentiating from prior studies that focus exclusively on memristors or PCMs alone and lack integrated energy-accuracy benchmarks under controlled neuromorphic training conditions.

topic: Energy-efficient neuromorphic computing
text:
IDEA:  
Integrating ferroelectric tunnel junctions (FTJs) with memristive synapses enables over 30% reduction in energy consumption during spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) learning in spiking neural networks, while maintaining classification accuracy within ±2% compared to memristor-only synapses.

BACKGROUND:  
Energy efficiency remains a critical bottleneck in neuromorphic computing, particularly during on-chip synaptic weight updates governed by STDP learning. Although memristor-based synapses offer promising low-power analog tuning, their nonlinearities and switching overhead limit further energy reduction. Hybrid synapses combining FTJs with memristors potentially leverage polarization-dependent tunneling resistance to reduce programming energy, but detailed device-level validation and theoretical justification for significant energy savings remain lacking.

APPROACH:  
We will develop a physics-calibrated hybrid synapse model integrating FTJ polarization switching dynamics with memristor conductance modulation to simulate realistic STDP-driven weight updates, including stochastic variability and asymmetric nonlinearities. The energy per synaptic event will be rigorously computed from measured device parameters of FTJs and memristors, and integrated within a crossbar-array simulation of a spiking neural network trained on the event-based N-MNIST dataset.

EXPERIMENT:  
We will compare total synaptic energy consumption and classification accuracy across full STDP training epochs for two architectures: a baseline using memristor-only synapses, and a proposed network with hybrid FTJ-memristor synapses. Success is defined by ≥30% reduction in synaptic energy consumption with classification accuracy within ±2% of the baseline on the N-MNIST test set, statistically verified over multiple randomized runs.

NOVELTY:  
This work uniquely combines experimentally derived FTJ device data with memristor models to provide the first analytically and empirically grounded demonstration of substantial synaptic energy savings exceeding 30%, while rigorously accounting for variability and accuracy-energy tradeoffs—advancing beyond prior memristor or hybrid synapse studies that lack such holistic device-system validation.

topic: Energy-efficient neuromorphic computing
text:
