IDEA: Integrating phase-change quantum materials with memristive synapses will reduce energy consumption per synaptic event by ≥30% compared to conventional ALD-deposited HfO₂ memristors under identical operational conditions in neuromorphic inference tasks.

BACKGROUND: Neuromorphic computing demands highly energy-efficient synaptic devices to emulate brain-like computation, yet existing memristive synapses, particularly HfO₂-based devices, face limits in reducing switching energy due to material and device physics constraints. Phase-change quantum materials exhibiting conductive phase transitions offer promising low-energy, non-volatile synaptic modulation mechanisms, but their energy-saving potential relative to established memristors remains experimentally unverified under rigorous benchmarking and variability controls.

APPROACH: Fabricate and integrate two matched synaptic arrays—one with conventional ALD-deposited HfO₂ memristors and one combining phase-change quantum materials (e.g., chalcogenide-based layers with engineered conductive phase transitions) with memristive elements—into identical neuromorphic circuits. Calibrate switching thresholds and dynamics precisely, then implement spiking neural networks trained offline on the N-MNIST dataset for real-time hardware-in-the-loop inference, measuring synaptic event energy with high-resolution, device-level electrical metrology under controlled temperature and cycling conditions.

EXPERIMENT: Benchmark average energy consumed per synaptic event during inference across the full N-MNIST test set, normalizing energy measurements to isolate synaptic switching from peripheral overhead. The hypothesis is confirmed if phase-change quantum synapses reduce energy per event by at least 30% relative to the HfO₂ baseline under matched voltage, spike frequency, and temperature; falsified if reductions are below 10%, with intermediate results deemed inconclusive pending further optimization.

NOVELTY: This work distinctly combines quantum material-driven conductive phase transitions with memristive synapses in a rigorously controlled hardware-software co-designed neuromorphic platform, providing the first statistically robust, device-level energy benchmarking against state-of-the-art ALD HfO₂ memristors; it elucidates physical mechanisms underlying energy savings and addresses practical integration challenges beyond prior demonstrations of PCM or memristor synapses alone.

topic: Quantum error correction in NISQ devices
text:
IDEA:  
Implementing adaptive, real-time feedback based on partial, repeated syndrome measurements combined with on-the-fly classical decoding on IBM’s 27-qubit Falcon processors will reduce logical error rates of encoded Quantum Volume circuits by at least 20% relative to fixed, precompiled QEC codes at comparable qubit overhead in NISQ devices.

BACKGROUND:  
NISQ devices suffer from high physical error rates and limited coherence times, limiting the practical benefits of standard fixed quantum error correction (QEC) codes, which often lack the flexibility to respond dynamically to detected errors. Existing QEC demonstrations on superconducting qubits typically employ fixed stabilizer measurements followed by offline decoding and recovery, but do not leverage mid-circuit measurement outcomes to perform low-latency, adaptive corrections. Bridging this gap is critical to improving logical qubit performance within current hardware constraints.

APPROACH:  
We propose an adaptive QEC scheme that performs partial, repeated syndrome extraction using mid-circuit measurements and conditional gates enabled by IBM Falcon hardware, paired with real-time classical decoding algorithms (e.g., optimized minimum-weight perfect matching) running within Qiskit Runtime to minimize feedback latency. This adaptive feedback triggers dynamic recovery operations during logical Quantum Volume (QV) circuit execution, contrasting with a baseline fixed code implementation of the [[7,1,3]] Steane or [[5,1,3]] code without intermediate corrections. Both approaches maintain near-identical qubit overhead (~7 qubits per logical qubit) and control for resource use.

EXPERIMENT:  
We will benchmark logical error rates by encoding QV circuits at various volumes (QV 8 and QV 16), executing at least 1000 shots per configuration to enable bootstrapped error estimation. Experiments include (1) fixed QEC with a single syndrome measurement and offline correction, (2) fixed QEC with repeated syndrome extraction but no adaptive corrections, and (3) adaptive QEC with real-time decoding and conditional recovery. Performance metrics are logical error rates (incorrect logical output probability), mid-circuit measurement fidelity, and total circuit runtime overhead. The hypothesis is falsified if adaptive QEC does not improve logical error rates by ≥20% relative to fixed QEC at similar qubit and latency overhead.

NOVELTY:  
This work uniquely integrates low-latency classical decoding via Qiskit Runtime with partial, repeated syndrome measurements to enable fully adaptive real-time corrections on publicly accessible superconducting NISQ hardware, surpassing prior demonstrations that rely on fixed decoding or offline correction. It rigorously benchmarks adaptive protocols against baseline fixed codes under realistic hardware latency and noise models, providing the first systematic experimental evidence on the practical advantage of adaptive QEC schemes tailored for NISQ-era constraints.

topic: Quantum error correction in NISQ devices
text:
IDEA: Implementing adaptive mid-circuit measurement-based feedback on NISQ superconducting devices reduces logical qubit error rates by at least 20% compared to state-of-the-art post-processing error mitigation alone under realistic latency and noise conditions.

BACKGROUND: Achieving practical quantum error correction on NISQ devices is challenged by limited qubit counts, short coherence times, and control latency, which constrain the utility of traditional QEC schemes. While post-processing error mitigation techniques partially alleviate errors, the potential advantage of real-time adaptive feedback via mid-circuit measurements remains unclear, especially when factoring in the overheads of measurement-induced errors and control delays. This work addresses the open problem of quantifying the practical benefit of such adaptive feedback under realistic device constraints.

APPROACH: We will implement the [[4,2,2]] error-detecting code on IBM Falcon-series processors (e.g., ibmq_toronto) using ancilla qubits for syndrome extraction and Qiskit runtime-enabled dynamic circuits to apply conditional Pauli corrections within the same circuit. The protocol explicitly quantifies and compensates for measurement and latency overhead by including control experiments with mid-circuit measurements but no feedback, allowing isolation of feedback benefits. Logical error rates will be extracted via syndrome-based logical error flags without full tomography, using a scalable decoding heuristic calibrated to device noise.

EXPERIMENT: We will benchmark three conditions—(1) raw logical qubit without mitigation, (2) logical qubit with standard post-processing error mitigation (readout error mitigation plus Pauli twirling), and (3) logical qubit with adaptive mid-circuit feedback—across a 6-state basis input set with ≥10,000 shots per state. Logical error rates per error detection cycle will be statistically compared using two-proportion z-tests (p < 0.01). Additional baselines include unencoded physical qubits and noise model simulations calibrated to device parameters to validate noise consistency and disentangle measurement overhead from feedback efficacy.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior demonstrations focusing mainly on static or partial mid-circuit feedback, this work systematically integrates realistic latency and measurement error budgets into the feedback protocol and decoding strategy on superconducting NISQ hardware, providing the first statistically rigorous quantification of feedback-induced logical error rate improvements beyond post-processing mitigation. The approach also advances a scalable, experimentally feasible decoding framework tailored to the [[4,2,2]] code, bridging theory and near-term device constraints with explicit performance benchmarks.

topic: Quantum error correction in NISQ devices
text:
IDEA:  
Implementing noise-tailored quantum error correction codes optimized for experimentally characterized correlated noise patterns in superconducting IBM Quantum NISQ devices will reduce logical error rates by at least 50% compared to generic QEC codes using standard independent noise assumptions.

BACKGROUND:  
Current quantum error correction (QEC) approaches for NISQ devices typically assume independent, identically distributed noise channels, failing to capture realistic spatial and temporal noise correlations inherent in superconducting qubit architectures. This mismatch limits error suppression effectiveness and impedes progress toward fault tolerance on NISQ hardware. Leveraging device-specific noise covariance data to design tailored stabilizers and correlated decoders remains an open problem with practical significance for near-term quantum computing.

APPROACH:  
We propose extracting up-to-date noise covariance matrices from IBM Quantum Experience calibration data (e.g., IBM Lagos and IBM Melbourne), incorporating temporal and spatial correlations into a noise-adapted QEC code design. Tailored stabilizer generators and syndrome measurement protocols will explicitly target correlated error syndromes, combined with advanced decoding algorithms such as correlated minimum-weight perfect matching to optimally decode error patterns. Real-time noise monitoring and adaptive recalibration protocols ensure robustness of noise models during experiments.

EXPERIMENT:  
We will simulate and benchmark logical error rates over 10,000 Monte Carlo runs for (1) the tailored QEC code and (2) two baselines: the [[5,1,3]] perfect code and a surface code of equivalent qubit count, both employing standard independent depolarizing noise models and state-of-the-art correlated noise decoders. Logical error rates under identical noise conditions reconstructed from IBM calibration datasets will be compared. Additionally, small instances of these codes will be implemented on IBM Quantum hardware with repeated syndrome extraction and error mitigation techniques, validated via randomized benchmarking and cross-entropy benchmarking metrics.

NOVELTY:  
This work advances beyond prior noise-adapted QEC studies by integrating continuous noise covariance tracking, hardware-compatible syndrome extraction respecting device constraints, and fair benchmarking with state-of-the-art decoders on realistic correlated noise channels. It rigorously quantifies logical error suppression gains with a fully specified experimental protocol and scalability analysis tailored to NISQ-era superconducting quantum processors.

topic: Quantum error correction in NISQ devices
text:
IDEA:  
Integrating a closed-loop adaptive quantum error correction (QEC) protocol that dynamically adjusts syndrome extraction frequency and decoding thresholds based on real-time noise diagnostics in superconducting NISQ devices will reduce logical error rates by more than 50% compared to static QEC schemes with fixed parameters.

BACKGROUND:  
NISQ devices suffer from time-varying noise and error mechanisms that limit the effectiveness of conventional, static QEC and error mitigation schemes, which do not adapt to changing noise profiles. Current adaptive QEC proposals often lack experimental validation under realistic hardware constraints, and it remains unclear whether adaptive strategies can significantly improve logical error rates beyond established baselines without incurring prohibitive overheads.

APPROACH:  
We develop an adaptive QEC control loop that continuously monitors noise parameters via interleaved randomized benchmarking and qubit calibration data on IBM Quantum Falcon processors, using these metrics to dynamically tune syndrome measurement frequency, leakage detection bases, and classical decoding thresholds in a [[5,1,3]] code implementation. This closed-loop approach aims to tailor error correction cycles to instantaneous noise profiles, balancing error suppression gains against measurement and feedback latency overheads quantified through a detailed error budget and timing analysis.

EXPERIMENT:  
We benchmark performance on OpenQASM circuits from the QASMBench dataset (Bernstein–Vazirani, Grover, QFT), comparing logical error rates over 10,000 runs between (1) static QEC with fixed syndrome schedules and noise-informed decoding thresholds, (2) state-of-the-art non-adaptive error mitigation (Pauli Twirling plus readout correction), and (3) the proposed adaptive QEC protocol. Statistical significance of logical error rate reductions exceeding 50% will be evaluated via bootstrap analysis (p < 0.05), while measuring overhead in execution time and syndrome measurement fidelity under varied environmental noise conditions.

NOVELTY:  
This work rigorously integrates real-time noise diagnostics with dynamic QEC parameter tuning validated on contemporary superconducting hardware, explicitly benchmarking against noise-aware static baselines and established error mitigation techniques. Unlike prior theoretical or simulation-only adaptive QEC proposals, it quantifies practical trade-offs and overheads, demonstrating adaptive QEC’s realistic potential for NISQ devices and delineating contexts where adaptation meaningfully outperforms fixed schemes.

topic: Quantum error correction in NISQ devices
text:
IDEA:  
Embedding adaptively updated, machine-learned noise models that incorporate real-time device calibration data into recurrent neural network decoders for quantum error correction on NISQ processors can yield up to 10% reduction in logical error rates compared to static decoders, while maintaining sub-10 ms decoding latency.

BACKGROUND:  
NISQ devices suffer from temporally varying noise characteristics that degrade the effectiveness of traditional QEC decoders relying on static noise assumptions, limiting logical error suppression. Existing decoders either ignore temporal noise drift or use fixed models, which fail to capture real-time device fluctuations. Addressing temporal noise variations with adaptive decoding could improve error detection fidelity but requires experimentally viable synchronization of syndrome and calibration data and low-latency decoding.

APPROACH:  
We propose training a recurrent neural network decoder that jointly processes syndrome measurement outcomes along with up-to-date, time-stamped qubit calibration parameters (T1, T2, gate and measurement error rates), continuously fine-tuned via a sliding window over recent calibration cycles to track noise drift. The decoder will be integrated within Qiskit Ignis, employing model compression and quantization to guarantee decoding under 10 ms, with offline training balanced by lightweight online fine-tuning to ensure real-time applicability.

EXPERIMENT:  
We will benchmark this adaptive decoder against a minimum-weight perfect matching (MWPM) decoder and a static, noise-agnostic neural-network decoder using syndrome datasets collected from IBM Quantum Hummingbird (27 qubits) and Falcon (65 qubits) processors running [[5,1,3]] and distance-3 and distance-5 surface codes over multiple days to capture temporal noise variations. Metrics include logical error rate reduction (target ≥8–10% improvement) and decoder latency (<10 ms), validated also on synthetic time-varying noise datasets generated with Qiskit Aer.

NOVELTY:  
This work pioneers a concrete, experimentally feasible protocol for synchronized, real-time acquisition and labeling of syndrome and calibration data with adaptive model updates under strict latency constraints, coupled with rigorous on-device and simulation benchmarking that isolates genuine adaptive decoding gains. Unlike prior approaches, it explicitly addresses temporal noise nonstationarity with recurrent architectures and integrates live device calibration streams, providing the first end-to-end adaptive QEC decoder demonstrated on contemporary NISQ processors with measured operational feasibility.

topic: Generative AI for drug discovery and molecular design
text:
IDEA:  
Integrating pathway-level biological network constraints via graph neural network embeddings into generative AI models improves the design of drug candidates with enhanced in vitro efficacy and reduced off-target toxicity compared to molecular structure-only generative approaches.

BACKGROUND:  
Current generative AI models for drug discovery primarily rely on molecular structure data and often neglect critical biological context, limiting their ability to predict compounds that effectively modulate disease-relevant pathways with minimal side effects. Incorporating pathway-level information that encodes protein interactions and metabolic dependencies may better guide molecule generation toward therapeutically relevant and safer candidates, addressing the challenge of improving translational success in early drug design.

APPROACH:  
We propose a conditional generative framework that fuses latent embeddings derived from graph neural networks processing curated human biological pathways (KEGG, Reactome) with molecular generators based on Transformer and VAE architectures trained on ChEMBL bioactivity data. This multi-modal integration is optimized via a composite loss balancing molecular validity, predicted binding/pathway node modulation, and minimized off-target toxicity (informed by PubChem BioAssay-trained predictors). Orthogonal pathway-specific functional assays and toxicity benchmarks using non-cancerous cell models will validate biological relevance and safety of generated compounds.

EXPERIMENT:  
We will benchmark the pathway-constrained generative models against baselines trained solely on molecular structures by synthesizing top-ranked molecules and assessing (1) in vitro efficacy via % growth inhibition on the NCI-60 panel and pathway-specific functional assays (e.g., phosphoproteomics reporter assays), and (2) off-target toxicity using selectivity indices derived from non-cancerous human cell lines and organoid models. Ablation studies with random or irrelevant pathway embeddings and conditioning controls will isolate the effect of biologically meaningful pathway integration. Success requires ≥15% improvement in growth inhibition and statistically significant (p < 0.05) enhancement in selectivity relative to baselines; failure to achieve ≥10% efficacy gain or improved selectivity falsifies the hypothesis.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior generative drug design efforts that focus on molecular structure alone or rely on static annotations, this approach explicitly integrates dynamic, pathway-level biological network constraints via graph neural embeddings into the generative process, combined with rigorous multi-objective optimization and orthogonal experimental validation. The inclusion of mechanistic functional assays and comprehensive ablation controls further distinguishes this work by directly linking pathway-aware generation to actionable biological outcomes.

topic: Generative AI for drug discovery and molecular design
text:
IDEA: Incorporating multi-modal data from indigenous Nigerian medicinal plant metabolomics and ethnobotanical usage metadata into a multi-encoder Transformer VAE will generate molecular candidates with significantly higher in vitro bioactivity hit rates than models trained solely on global chemical databases.

BACKGROUND: Current generative AI models for drug discovery typically rely on large global chemical databases like ChEMBL but often overlook rich, contextualized data from indigenous medicinal plants and traditional therapeutic knowledge. Integrating metabolomic profiles with curated ethnobotanical metadata offers an underexploited opportunity to embed biologically relevant, culturally contextual information that may bias molecular generation toward bioactive compounds aligned with traditional medicine, addressing limitations in both chemical diversity and therapeutic relevance.

APPROACH: We propose a multi-modal generative modeling framework combining metabolomics data from the Nigerian Indigenous Medicinal Plant Metabolome (NIMPM) database and ontology-encoded traditional usage metadata with ChEMBL chemical structures using a multi-encoder Transformer VAE architecture. The model’s encoders separately process molecular graphs and textual metadata embeddings, which are fused in the latent space for joint representation learning. Reinforcement learning fine-tunes molecule generation toward drug-likeness, synthetic accessibility, and expected bioactivity, while a robust data curation and validation pipeline ensures high-quality, biologically meaningful embeddings.

EXPERIMENT: We will train two models—a baseline Transformer VAE on ChEMBL 30 alone, and the multi-modal model on combined NIMPM metabolomics, ethnobotanical metadata, and ChEMBL data—and generate candidate molecules. Compounds prioritized through retrosynthetic feasibility analysis and synthetic accessibility scoring will be synthesized or procured and tested in well-controlled, standardized in vitro assays reflecting traditional therapeutic targets (e.g., anti-inflammatory, antimalarial, antimicrobial). Statistical analysis (Fisher’s exact test, p < 0.05) will compare hit rates (IC50 < 10 μM) between models, with a predefined success threshold of at least a 20% increase in bioactivity rate for the multi-modal model to confirm the hypothesis.

NOVELTY: This work uniquely integrates high-resolution indigenous metabolomics with rigorously encoded traditional usage metadata into a multi-encoder generative model architecture—moving beyond prior studies that either use local data without standardized multi-modal fusion or rely solely on global databases. The incorporation of a detailed data preprocessing pipeline, ontology-based metadata embeddings, and a comprehensive experimental validation strategy to directly link culturally contextualized data with improved molecular bioactivity rates constitutes a novel advancement in AI-driven drug discovery.

topic: Generative AI for drug discovery and molecular design
text:
IDEA:  
Diffusion-based generative models trained on rigorously aligned multi-modal datasets combining molecular structures and bioactivity assay images will significantly outperform transformer-based models in generating novel drug-like molecules with experimentally validated bioactivity.

BACKGROUND:  
Current generative AI methods for drug discovery predominantly rely on unimodal molecular data such as SMILES strings or molecular graphs, limiting their ability to integrate heterogeneous biological context like assay imaging. Furthermore, transformer-based models, while powerful for sequence data, face challenges in jointly modeling discrete molecular structures and complex visual bioactivity data, constraining their predictive accuracy for bioactive molecule design. Addressing these limitations by leveraging multi-modal data integration remains an open problem with high potential impact on discovering efficacious novel drugs.

APPROACH:  
We propose to develop a conditional guided denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) architecture that jointly encodes molecular graph embeddings and bioactivity assay image features via cross-attention conditioned U-Nets. This multi-modal diffusion model will be trained on a newly curated, quantitatively validated paired dataset aligning MOSES molecular structures with ChEMBL bioassay microscopy images and activity annotations. We will directly compare this diffusion approach to state-of-the-art transformer-based baselines including unimodal Chemformer models and multi-modal Chemformer variants incorporating assay image embeddings, all trained under matched computational budgets.

EXPERIMENT:  
We will align MOSES and ChEMBL datasets to create a multi-modal training set of (molecular structure, assay image) pairs with bioactivity labels, validating overlap and data quality statistically. Models will be evaluated on chemical validity, novelty, and critically the Pearson correlation between predicted and experimentally measured bioactivity scores on held-out test molecules. Success is defined as the diffusion model improving bioactivity prediction correlation by ≥10% over the best transformer baseline; failure is defined as <5% improvement or worse performance, thereby falsifying the hypothesis.

NOVELTY:  
This work is the first to rigorously integrate and jointly model molecular graph and bioactivity assay image data in a diffusion generative framework for drug design, overcoming discrete data and heterogeneous modality fusion challenges that limit transformer-based approaches. It includes a novel dataset alignment strategy and experimentally grounded evaluation with explicit bioactivity validation criteria, advancing beyond prior unimodal or sequence-only generative models.

topic: Generative AI for drug discovery and molecular design
text:
IDEA: Incorporating experimentally derived protein conformational ensembles as explicit conditioning inputs into transformer-based generative AI models will yield drug candidates with significantly improved binding affinity and selectivity compared to models trained on single static protein structures.

BACKGROUND: Traditional generative AI approaches for drug discovery largely rely on static protein structures that fail to capture the dynamic nature of protein binding sites, limiting the accuracy of predicted ligand interactions. Experimentally derived conformational ensembles from NMR or MD better represent protein flexibility and may provide richer context for drug design, yet their integration into generative frameworks remains underexplored and unvalidated with rigorous benchmarks.

APPROACH: We propose encoding multiple experimentally validated protein conformers from the Protein Ensemble Database into a multi-input embedding layer that conditions a transformer-based molecular generator (e.g., REINVENT 4). Ensemble docking scores generated via flexible docking (AutoDock Vina) across conformers will be aggregated and incorporated alongside known ligand data to train the model via reinforcement learning with a composite reward emphasizing mean binding affinity and selectivity against off-target ensembles. Orthogonal validation via free energy perturbation calculations and experimental binding assays will augment docking-based metrics.

EXPERIMENT: We will benchmark >10 pharmaceutically relevant targets (kinases, GPCRs, nuclear receptors) using PED for ensembles and PDB for static structures, training two parallel models: one conditioned on static structures and one on ensemble representations. Success criteria include ≥1 kcal/mol improvement in predicted binding affinity, ≥20% improvement in selectivity ratios, and ≥0.05 increase in retrospective classification AUROC on blinded test sets of known actives/inactives, supplemented by prospective synthesis and biophysical validation of top candidates.

NOVELTY: This work rigorously integrates experimentally derived conformational ensembles directly into generative AI conditioning, advancing beyond prior ensemble docking or generative modeling efforts by combining multi-conformer encoding, uncertainty-aware reward functions, and orthogonal high-fidelity validation to conclusively demonstrate the practical advantage of protein dynamics in AI-driven drug design.

topic: Generative AI for drug discovery and molecular design
text:
IDEA:  
Integrating protein target structural variation informed by human pharmacogenomic variants with indigenous medicinal plant metabolomics into a multi-branch generative AI model will yield novel drug candidates exhibiting significantly enhanced target specificity and pharmacogenomic relevance compared to models trained on chemical structure data alone.

BACKGROUND:  
Current generative AI approaches for drug discovery largely rely on chemical structure data without explicitly incorporating host genetic variation that modulates drug response and target binding. Indigenous medicinal plant metabolomics represent an underexploited, chemically diverse resource, but prior models have not integrated this with biologically contextualized human genomic variation. Addressing this gap can improve the design of drug candidates with higher specificity tailored to population-level genetic diversity, thus advancing precision pharmacology.

APPROACH:  
We propose a multi-modal generative AI framework based on REINVENT 4 architecture augmented by a multi-branch neural network encoding: (1) indigenous Nigerian plant metabolomics embeddings derived from high-resolution mass spectrometry, (2) protein target structural embeddings capturing variant-induced binding site alterations from pharmacogenomic loci (e.g., CYP450, HLA), linked to human genomic variant data via variant impact scores. This biologically informed integration enables the model to generate molecules optimized for both chemical novelty and genotype-aware target binding. Ablation studies will isolate contributions of each modality and embedding strategy.

EXPERIMENT:  
Using three datasets—(1) Nigerian Indigenous Medicinal Plant Metabolomics (African Plant Metomics Initiative), (2) 1000 Genomes Project Phase 3 focusing on pharmacogenomic variants mapped to protein binding site structures, and (3) ChEMBL 29 as baseline—we will train baseline models (REINVENT 4 on ChEMBL alone and ChEMBL plus metabolomics) and the proposed multi-modal model. Candidate molecules (10,000 each) will be assessed by docking via AutoDock Vina to a panel of 50 pharmacogenomically relevant protein targets with variant-specific structures. Primary metrics include target specificity ratio (>1.5-fold improvement over baseline), binding affinity, novelty (Tanimoto <0.4), synthetic accessibility (SA score <4), and orthogonal validation by molecular dynamics simulations. Statistical significance will be evaluated by Wilcoxon signed-rank tests (p < 0.05). Failure to outperform baselines or generate practically accessible molecules falsifies the hypothesis.

NOVELTY:  
This work uniquely combines explicit protein structural context of pharmacogenomic variants with indigenous plant metabolomics in a unified generative AI framework, moving beyond prior models that treat genomic data as population-level embeddings without mechanistic binding site linkage. The integration strategy and comprehensive validation protocol provide a robust, interpretable approach for pharmacogenomically informed de novo drug design, specifically leveraging underrepresented chemical diversity from African medicinal plants.

topic: Uncertainty quantification in deep neural networks
text:
IDEA:  
Incorporate learned data manifold geometry from supervised contrastive representation learning into uncertainty quantification frameworks to reduce miscalibration and improve out-of-distribution detection more effectively than ensemble or Bayesian methods alone.

BACKGROUND:  
Deep neural networks often produce poorly calibrated uncertainty estimates, especially on out-of-distribution (OOD) data, limiting their reliability in safety-critical applications. Conventional uncertainty quantification (UQ) methods—such as MC-Dropout, Deep Ensembles, and Bayesian Neural Networks—provide uncertainty estimates but may fail to capture the intrinsic geometric structure of in-distribution data, which is crucial for robust OOD detection and calibration. Leveraging learned manifold representations via contrastive learning could bridge this gap by explicitly modeling data geometry to inform uncertainty estimation.

APPROACH:  
We propose a UQ framework that first trains a ResNet-50 encoder with supervised contrastive learning (SupCon loss) to learn a robust embedding of the in-distribution data manifold. Subsequently, uncertainty scores are computed post-hoc via Mahalanobis distance or a lightweight Gaussian Mixture Model fitted on these embeddings, reflecting geometric consistency with the training distribution. This contrasts with baselines—MC-Dropout, Deep Ensembles (5 models), and variational Bayesian neural networks—each producing uncertainty via predictive entropy or mutual information on the same ResNet-50 backbone, enabling direct comparison on a common scale.

EXPERIMENT:  
We will evaluate on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 as in-distribution datasets and SVHN, LSUN (cropped), and Tiny-ImageNet (cropped) as OOD benchmarks, measuring Expected Calibration Error (ECE) on OOD detection, AUROC, and False Positive Rate at 95% True Positive Rate (FPR95). Success requires the proposed contrastive manifold-based approach to achieve at least a 20% relative reduction in ECE and a 5% absolute increase in AUROC against all three baselines averaged across OOD datasets, with joint training and uncertainty estimation protocols rigorously controlled and matched.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior work that treats uncertainty estimation and representation learning independently, this method explicitly integrates learned geometric structure of the data manifold into the uncertainty scoring, backed by theoretical motivation linking contrastive embeddings to calibrated uncertainty. The approach is distinct from ensemble and Bayesian methods by leveraging geometry-aware embeddings for post-hoc uncertainty quantification, supported by intermediate embedding quality controls and robustness checks to isolate representation quality from uncertainty estimation effects.

topic: Uncertainty quantification in deep neural networks
text:
IDEA: Incorporating trainable heteroscedastic noise layers within a ResNet-18 architecture improves uncertainty calibration on out-of-distribution data compared to Bayesian neural networks with fixed Gaussian priors and Monte Carlo dropout baselines.

BACKGROUND: Deep neural networks often produce poorly calibrated uncertainty estimates under distributional shift, limiting their reliability in safety-critical applications. While Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) and Monte Carlo dropout (MC dropout) address epistemic uncertainty with fixed priors or stochastic regularization, they frequently underperform in capturing input-dependent aleatoric uncertainty that varies across samples. Improving uncertainty quantification, particularly under out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions, remains an open challenge.

APPROACH: We propose augmenting a ResNet-18 classifier with parallel trainable heteroscedastic noise layers, implemented as a subnetwork predicting input-dependent variance parameters for a heteroscedastic Gaussian likelihood. This enables end-to-end learning of aleatoric uncertainty alongside classification, optimizing a negative log-likelihood loss. Predictive uncertainty is derived by combining softmax predictive probabilities with learned heteroscedastic variance in a principled probabilistic framework, explicitly modeling aleatoric uncertainty complementary to epistemic uncertainty.

EXPERIMENT: Models will be trained on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 as in-distribution datasets and evaluated on SVHN and Tiny ImageNet (resized to 32×32) as OOD benchmarks. Baselines include a variational inference Bayesian ResNet-18 with fixed Gaussian weight priors and MC Dropout ResNet-18, all carefully tuned with matched architectures and hyperparameters. Calibration will be assessed using Expected Calibration Error (ECE), Negative Log Likelihood (NLL), and Brier score on both in-distribution and OOD data. Statistical significance of calibration improvements will be evaluated via paired t-tests (p < 0.05), while monitoring classification accuracy to detect potential trade-offs.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior work that treats aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty separately or relies on fixed prior assumptions in BNNs, this approach explicitly learns input-dependent noise variance within a heteroscedastic framework integrated end-to-end, enabling flexible adaptation to varying data uncertainty. This provides a theoretically grounded and empirically validated mechanism for improved OOD calibration beyond existing Bayesian or MC dropout methods.

topic: Uncertainty quantification in deep neural networks
text:
IDEA: Incorporating explicit causal structure priors into Bayesian neural networks via modular hierarchical priors significantly improves uncertainty quantification on out-of-distribution samples, reducing overconfident predictions compared to MC dropout and deep ensembles.

BACKGROUND: Deep neural networks often produce overconfident uncertainty estimates when exposed to out-of-distribution (OOD) data, limiting their reliability in safety-critical scenarios. While Bayesian neural networks (BNNs), MC dropout, and ensembles offer uncertainty quantification, they typically treat models as black boxes without leveraging known causal relationships, missing opportunities to improve robustness under distributional shifts induced by causal interventions.

APPROACH: We propose a Bayesian modular neural network architecture where the network is factorized into modules aligned with variables in a known causal graph, and hierarchical Bayesian priors encode the conditional dependencies dictated by causal relations. Posterior inference is performed using scalable variational inference or Hamiltonian Monte Carlo to capture structured uncertainty consistent with the causal graph, enabling principled propagation of uncertainty through causally-informed subnetworks.

EXPERIMENT: We evaluate on CMNIST and CelebA datasets with rigorously constructed OOD test sets generated by systematic causal interventions (e.g., changing color-label correlations in CMNIST and altering attribute co-occurrences in CelebA). We compare Causal-BNNs against MC dropout and 5-member deep ensembles on identical backbones, measuring Expected Calibration Error (ECE), Negative Log Likelihood (NLL), Brier score, OOD detection AUROC, and the proportion of OOD samples predicted with >0.9 confidence. Ablation studies isolate the impact of causal priors from modularity and Bayesian inference.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior work on uncertainty quantification that treats neural networks monolithically or uses generic Bayesian priors, our method explicitly integrates known causal structure into the Bayesian framework, providing a theoretically grounded mechanism for improved uncertainty calibration under causally induced distribution shifts. This bridges causal representation learning and Bayesian uncertainty quantification, offering novel insights into robust OOD detection and overconfidence mitigation.

topic: Uncertainty quantification in deep neural networks
text:
IDEA:  
Using a structured latent variable model that explicitly disentangles aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty in deep neural networks improves calibration and out-of-distribution detection performance beyond state-of-the-art Bayesian and ensemble methods.

BACKGROUND:  
Current uncertainty quantification methods in deep neural networks, such as MC-Dropout, Deep Ensembles, and Bayesian Neural Networks, often conflate aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties, limiting interpretability and calibration, especially under distribution shifts. Distinguishing these uncertainty types is crucial for reliable decision-making in ambiguous in-distribution data and challenging out-of-distribution settings. However, rigorous, quantifiable disentanglement and its direct impact on improved predictive uncertainty remain open problems.

APPROACH:  
We propose a latent variable model integrating a Variational Autoencoder-style architecture with a ResNet-18 classifier, employing separate latent variables and inference networks to explicitly model aleatoric uncertainty (inherent data noise, e.g., label ambiguity) and epistemic uncertainty (model uncertainty due to limited or OOD data). Training optimizes a joint evidence lower bound (ELBO) with structured priors that enforce disentanglement, enabling distinct sampling-based estimates of each uncertainty type. Quantitative disentanglement metrics are developed to validate the unique correspondence of latents to uncertainty sources.

EXPERIMENT:  
We train and evaluate on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 with controlled 20% symmetric label noise for aleatoric uncertainty assessment, and test OOD calibration using SVHN and TinyImageNet (32x32). Baselines include MC-Dropout, Deep Ensembles (5 models), and Bayesian Neural Networks via Variational Inference, all using comparable ResNet-18 architectures. Metrics include Expected Calibration Error (ECE) separately computed on noisy in-distribution and clean OOD data, and AUROC for OOD detection based on combined uncertainty scores. Multiple independent runs with statistical significance testing and confidence intervals will confirm improvements, while disentanglement validation uses proxy ground truth (noise injection) and latent space statistics.

NOVELTY:  
This work provides the first rigorously quantifiable and reproducible framework for explicit and identifiable disentanglement of aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty via structured latent variables in deep classifiers, together with theoretical justification and empirical evidence that such disentanglement yields significantly improved OOD calibration and detection beyond existing Bayesian and ensemble approaches.

topic: Uncertainty quantification in deep neural networks
text:
IDEA: Incorporate learned latent input data manifold geometry as a conformity-guided uncertainty modulator within Bayesian and ensemble uncertainty quantification frameworks to reduce overconfident uncertainty estimates under distributional shifts and OOD inputs.

BACKGROUND: Deep neural networks often produce overconfident uncertainty estimates, especially for inputs lying off the training data manifold or under distribution shift, limiting their reliability in safety-critical applications. While Bayesian and ensemble methods improve uncertainty quantification (UQ), they lack explicit mechanisms to penalize predictions on inputs that deviate from the learned data geometry, leading to calibration failures and poor OOD detection.

APPROACH: We propose first learning a low-dimensional latent manifold of clean training data via a variational or denoising autoencoder, rigorously validating its stability and representativeness across clean, corrupted, and OOD inputs. During inference, we compute a manifold conformity score using the Mahalanobis distance (or an empirically justified alternative) in latent space from each input to the manifold distribution and integrate this score as a post-hoc uncertainty modulator on top of Bayesian neural networks or deep ensembles. Ablations and strong novelty-detection baselines (e.g., Mahalanobis distance in input/feature space and ODIN) will isolate the contribution of learned manifold geometry.

EXPERIMENT: We evaluate on CIFAR-10-C for calibration under varying corruption severities and on CelebA-HQ demographic bias subsets for OOD detection, using Expected Calibration Error (ECE), Negative Log Likelihood (NLL), and Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve (AUROC). Success requires ≥10% relative improvement in ECE and NLL over the best baseline across conditions and AUROC > 0.9 for out-of-manifold inputs, with statistical rigor including error bars, severity stratification, and power analyses.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior work that applies uncertainty estimation or OOD detection without explicit geometry-informed uncertainty modulation, this method uniquely integrates a validated latent manifold conformity measure as a principled, post-hoc uncertainty recalibration layer atop standard Bayesian and ensemble models, providing both theoretical and empirical evidence linking manifold deviation to overconfident uncertainty errors.
